articles.title: 5 Alternatives To Ledger To Store Your Bitcoin
articles.text:
5 alternatives to Ledger to store your Bitcoin
Hardware wallets aren’t the only way to protect your crypto, but from ETFs and passkeys to multisig accounts, each alternative has its own risks and trade-offs.
After more than $200 million dollars worth of crypto was stolen in recent months from tampered Ledgers, and Coldcards where the seed generated wasn’t truly random, faith in hardware wallets has been shaken to the core.  
These Bitcoin and crypto holders did everything right. They bought the products from official sources, correctly stored their seed phrases and they trusted in the phrase “not your keys, not your coins”, but they lost out any way. The thefts suggest that even the most diligent crypto holder using a hardware wallet faces risks beyond their control.
With the number of physical attacks on crypto holders rising — there’s been a $5 wrench attack in France every 2.5 days this year — the drawbacks of storing crypto on a hardware wallet are becoming clearer. And that’s even before you consider how many crypto owners have lost wallets and seed phrases over the years — “boating accidents” for tax purposes excluded.
There are plenty of drawbacks with all of the alternative methods of holding crypto however, so spreading your stack across different addresses and via different methods will at least minimize the damage if any one method is compromised.
Here are five alternatives for storing your crypto.
1. Crypto ETFs: Trusting BlackRock may now be an option
The first and most important caveat to this hardware wallet alternative is that it isn’t technically a way to store crypto at all. Even if you deposit Bitcoin directly, it is exchanged for shares in a financial product that holds crypto assets through a custodian. You end up with a claim on the ETF’s net asset value in dollars, not in Bitcoin. So there are trade offs.
On the one hand, using crypto exchange-traded funds (ETFs) removes many of the headaches associated with direct ownership, like protecting your seed phrase, backing up your wallet or worrying about every knock at the door.
On the other hand, crypto ETFs present their own risks, like trusting a centralized provider, third-party custody arrangements, fees and potential deviations between the share price and the digital asset’s market price.
Crypto ETFs have their own risks. Source: SEC
Ophelia Snyder, co-founder of asset manager 21Shares, tells Magazine that exchange-traded products make more sense “for most people most of the time” due to “tax, estate planning and security reasons.”
Related: Can crypto users trust the supply chain behind hardware wallets?
However, the “ability to use crypto onchain” and “some risk exposure to the issuer” are among the main trade-offs. She also says that security depends on the provider, and the controls around its wallet infrastructure should be a “major factor” when choosing a product.
Pseudonymous Bitcoin stock-to-flow (S2F) model creator PlanB moved his BTC to ETFs in 2025 and said he was widely criticized for that decision. After the Ledger and Coldcard incidents, however, he said, “Zero regrets of my ETF decision. Peace of mind.”
2. Passkey-based wallets: Move away from seed phrase management
Passkeys let users access accounts with a cryptographic credential stored on a device (typically a phone via Apple or Google passkeys), often protected by a fingerprint, face scan or PIN. Unlike hardware wallets, they don’t require a dedicated device to keep crypto keys offline. Passkeys are more common for chains that have smart contracts.
Some passkey-based options include Coinbase Wallet’s Smart Wallet, Clave and Infinex, with differing designs and recovery options.
While passkeys may provide a smoother user experience, they aren’t a panacea; losing a device or passkey can still create problems, so users should check how backups work and whether recovering access requires trusting a third party.
In June 2024, Adam Back, chief executive of Bitcoin infrastructure provider Blockstream, questioned Coinbase’s Smart Wallet, asking what would happen if a passkey were hacked; “sounds like basically a hosted wallet with a better sales pitch,” he said.
3. Multisig wallets: Split control across multiple keys
As the name implies, a multisignature wallet requires multiple keys to authorize a transaction. In common 2-of-3 setups, three separate signers hold keys, and any two must approve a transaction before funds can move.
Multisig can reduce reliance on a single key or device, but it doesn’t always eliminate the need for a hardware wallet. Casa, for example, offers multisignature custody for individuals and families, with a setup combining a hardware wallet, a mobile phone and a key held by Casa.
PlanB says no regrets moving BTC to an ETF. Source: PlanB
Many of the largest Ethereum ecosystem projects manage their treasuries via Safe wallet (formerly Gnosis Safe) — an on chain smart account multisig with a web based interface.
While that setup can reduce the risk of a single compromised or lost key, multisig arrangements have disadvantages too.
Multiple-person setups, for example, need the signers to remain available, while smart contract wallets can introduce vulnerabilities in their code or configuration, and an attacker who compromises enough signers can still authorize a transaction.
Related: Coldcard says it’s investigating how phishing link appeared on its X account
Coordinating approvals can also slow down transfers, which can be unhelpful when time is of the essence, particularly when signers are in different locations and time zones.
Casa chief executive Nick Neuman told Cointelegraph earlier this month that, even with a multisig setup, users should still spread their risk across multiple providers rather than rely on just one.
4. Centralized exchanges: Let someone else handle custody
Keeping crypto on a centralized exchange transfers the responsibility for private key management to a company and removes most of the burden of being responsible for your own security. It’s certainly more convenient for active traders or holders who don’t want to manage backups and recovery phrases.
But the old refrain “not your keys, not your coins” is particularly pertinent here. Crypto’s short history is littered with incidents of exchange hacks and exploits, from owners taking access to user assets with them to their graves to one of the largest BTC hacks in history, with investors still waiting to recover their coins 13 years later.
Of course, centralized exchange operational security has come a long way, and many now publish proof-of-reserves reports or have emergency funds to help cover losses.
Many centralized exchanges publish proof-of-reserves reports. Source: Binance
That said, proof of reserves doesn’t actually establish a company’s full financial health or ability to meet every obligation.
And with the rise in crypto reporting requirements, including through the OECD’s Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework, exchanges require customers to provide identity, residency or tax information, and failure to comply can lead to account restrictions or suspended withdrawals.
5. Paper wallets: Offline but not necessarily safer
A paper wallet traditionally consists of a cryptocurrency address and its corresponding private key printed on paper.
While paper wallets keep key material offline without requiring a dedicated hardware device, generating one safely can be difficult, as a compromised computer, malicious generator or poor source of randomness can expose the key before it is printed.
And of course, paper can also be easily lost or damaged; you definitely don’t want to smoke a celebratory cigar next to this form of crypto storage (stamping the seed onto metal is a good alternative however). Spending funds can also compromise security if the private key is imported into an internet-connected wallet.
So while paper wallets are an alternative to hardware wallets, for most users, they simply aren’t a better one, and are a poor fit compared with more manageable offline-storage options.
At the end of the day, there is no one ideal way to store your crypto, and for every holder, it will come down to their personal circumstances and needs. As Snyder says:
“Self-custody users have a tendency to be in two camps: either long-term crypto natives who have a strong view on their personal security practices and everyone else.”
If you aren’t in the first group, she says, self-custody may generally not be the best fit for you, and having some crypto on a centralized exchange and an ETF can be “a really useful tool as part of a portfolio approach to holding crypto.”
Magazine: ‘Bunker mode’ won’t protect your crypto, critics say

articles.title: OCC Issues Final Stablecoin Rule Under GENIUS Act
articles.text:
OCC finalizes GENIUS Act rules for stablecoin issuers and custody
The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency’s final rule covers payment stablecoin issuance and some custody activities, with the GENIUS Act framework taking effect in mid-January.
The US Office of the Comptroller of the Currency finalized rules Wednesday for payment stablecoin reserves, redemptions and related custody activities, implementing the GENIUS Act for entities under its jurisdiction.
The final rule states issuers must maintain reserves worth at least as much as their outstanding stablecoins and generally process redemption requests within two business days.
The rule applies to national banks, federal savings associations and federal branches and their subsidiaries, as well as nonbank firms that seek or receive federal qualified issuer status, according to the agency’s announcement. It also covers state-qualified issuers when the OCC has regulatory or enforcement authority over them.
The rule and the GENIUS Act will take effect Jan. 18, 2027.
“We are providing a clear, practical framework for payment stablecoin innovation, with strong standards for reserve backing, redemption, and risk management,” Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan Gould said.
The OCC dropped a proposed presumption that certain arrangements involving affiliates or related third parties violate the law’s yield ban. The final rule retains the ban on issuers paying holders interest or yield solely for holding, using or retaining their stablecoins. The agency said it retains authority to act against attempts to evade that prohibition.
The OCC said it will announce separately when it begins processing issuer applications and waiver requests; the agency and Treasury will address Bank Secrecy Act, anti-money-laundering and sanctions requirements in separate rulemaking.

articles.title: Musk’s SpaceX-Tesla Merger Would Create a Bitcoin Treasury Behemoth - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- Elon Musk’s floated SpaceX-Tesla merger would unite the companies’ combined 30,221 BTC, worth roughly $2.5 billion, into one of the largest non-mining corporate Bitcoin treasuries.
- SpaceX’s stash was effectively invisible to public markets until its June IPO filing, having quietly accumulated for years.
- Musk cautioned a deal isn’t “a certainty,” and neither company has signaled buying or selling.
Elon Musk’s floated merger of SpaceX and Tesla would do more than unite rockets and electric cars. It would fold two of the world’s largest corporate Bitcoin stashes onto a single balance sheet.
Speaking on SpaceX’s third-quarter earnings call Tuesday, Musk said the boards of both companies had formed special committees of independent directors to weigh a tie-up, cautioning that treating a deal as “a certainty” would be “overstating it.”
But the prospect alone has drawn fresh attention to the combined entity’s crypto holdings.
Tesla reported 11,509 BTC in its most recent quarterly filing, while SpaceX disclosed 18,712 BTC in the S-1 it filed ahead of its June IPO. Together, that’s 30,221 BTC, worth roughly $2.5 billion at Bitcoin’s recent price near $83,000.
As Decrypt reported when the merger idea first surfaced, combining the two would stack one of the largest non-mining corporate Bitcoin positions anywhere under Musk’s control, placing the merged company among the top handful of public holders, trailing only the likes of Michael Saylor’s Strategy and a few others.
The SpaceX portion is the more striking piece. The rocket maker’s 18,712 BTC was effectively invisible to public markets until its IPO filing, meaning a substantial treasury had quietly accumulated inside a private company for years before anyone could count it, more than double what blockchain trackers had previously attributed to SpaceX wallets. The combined cost basis across both firms sits around $1 billion, implying an average buy price near $35,000 per coin.
A merger wouldn’t change anything about Bitcoin itself, and neither company has signaled plans to buy or sell. Both have held their positions static, with SpaceX last moving coins in prior years and Tesla reporting no changes.
What a deal would alter is governance and accounting: one of the most closely watched corporate Bitcoin piles would sit inside a single public vehicle, subject to quarterly disclosures and the fair-value accounting that recently forced Tesla to book a loss as Bitcoin slid.
For now, the treasury math is hypothetical, living or dying with a transaction that remains exploratory. But it underscores how, almost incidentally, a Musk mega-merger would also create a Bitcoin giant.

articles.title: What Is a Bitcoin-Backed Loan? Borrowing Against BTC Explained - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- Bitcoin-backed loans let holders pledge BTC as collateral to borrow dollars or stablecoins, keeping exposure to Bitcoin's price and often avoiding a taxable sale.
- Loan-to-value ratios typically run from about 30% to 70%, and borrowers face margin calls or liquidation if Bitcoin's price falls sharply.
- The market has matured since the 2022 lender collapses, with an investment-grade securitization and big banks joining in, though published rates still run from about 5.8% to 14%.
Most long-term Bitcoin holders know this problem. You need cash for a house deposit, a business or a tax bill, but selling BTC means giving up exposure to its future price. In many countries it also means paying capital gains tax. A Bitcoin-backed loan is a way around that: you pledge your Bitcoin as collateral and borrow dollars or stablecoins against it.
The idea is as old as lending itself. People have long borrowed against homes, stock portfolios and gold. What's new is the collateral, an asset that trades around the clock and can swing in price by double digits in a week.
The market collapsed in 2022, when lenders including Celsius and BlockFi went bankrupt. It has since come back in a more cautious form, with centralized lending more than tripling from its late-2023 low, according to Galaxy Research.
This guide covers what Bitcoin-backed loans are, how they work, who offers them, and the risks borrowers should understand before taking one out.
What is a Bitcoin-backed loan?
A Bitcoin-backed loan is a secured loan with BTC as the collateral. You deposit Bitcoin with a lender, or lock it in a smart contract. In return you get a loan worth a fraction of that Bitcoin's value, paid in fiat currency such as U.S. dollars or in a stablecoin such as USDC.
While the loan is open, your Bitcoin stays locked. Once you repay the principal plus interest, you get it back.
Lenders lean on the collateral rather than your income history, so many of these loans need little or no traditional credit check. They come in two broad types:
- Centralized (CeFi) loans, from companies such as Ledn, Strike, Unchained, Nexo and Coinbase. You go through identity checks, and the company or its custodian holds your BTC.
- Decentralized (DeFi) loans, from protocols such as Aave and Morpho. A smart contract holds the collateral, and native BTC usually has to be "wrapped" into a token on another blockchain first.
Did you know?
Wrapped Bitcoin is a token on another blockchain, such as Ethereum, that is backed 1:1 by real BTC held in custody. It enables Bitcoin to be used in DeFi apps.
How does a Bitcoin-backed loan work?
The key number is the loan-to-value (LTV) ratio: how much you borrow compared with the value of your collateral. Industry LTVs typically range from about 30% to 70%, and many lenders start at 50%. At a 50% LTV, $100,000 of Bitcoin gets you a $50,000 loan.
That cushion matters because Bitcoin is volatile. If BTC's price falls, your LTV rises. Lenders set thresholds:
- Margin call: if your LTV rises past a set level, you're asked to add more collateral or repay part of the loan.
- Liquidation: if the LTV keeps rising, the lender sells some or all of your Bitcoin to cover the debt. In DeFi, smart contracts do this automatically.
Terms vary. Some products have fixed 12-month terms with monthly interest. Others, such as Coinbase's loans, have no monthly payments and no repayment deadline. Interest simply builds up on the balance.
Did you know?
"Rehypothecation" means a lender re-lends your collateral to someone else to earn extra yield. It was a big reason customers of failed lenders in 2022 lost their deposits.
What's so special about Bitcoin-backed loans?
The main draw is getting cash while keeping your Bitcoin. In many jurisdictions, borrowing is not a taxable event, but selling is. Check your local rules, though.
The sector has also matured. Lenders now advertise that they don't rehypothecate collateral, and some offer "collaborative custody." Unchained, for example, keeps loan collateral in a 2-of-3 multisig vault: the borrower, Unchained and an independent key agent each hold one key, and no single party can move the coins alone.
Wall Street is paying attention too. In February 2026, Ledn closed a $188 million Bitcoin-backed asset-backed securitization. S&P Global assigned its $160 million senior class a preliminary "BBB-" rating, which SVB described as the first investment-grade rating for a Bitcoin-collateralized lending portfolio. Galaxy put total crypto-backed loan volume at $56.16 billion in Q2 2026, down 16.8% from the previous quarter as borrowers cut back on leverage, with centralized lenders now holding more loans than DeFi protocols.
Did you know?
Coinbase has passed $1 billion in Bitcoin-backed loan originations, according to the company.
Who's offering Bitcoin-backed loans?
- 🏦 Ledn: a Bitcoin-focused lender with custodied loans whose collateral isn't lent out.
- 🔐 Unchained: commercial loans held in multisig vaults where the borrower holds a key.
- ⚡ Strike: Bitcoin-backed loans for individuals and businesses in select U.S. states.
- 🔵 Coinbase: on-chain loans run through the Morpho protocol, available in most U.S. states.
- 💳 Aven: launched a Bitcoin-backed Visa credit line in April 2026 with limits up to $1 million.
- 🌐 Nexo: instant credit lines against BTC and 100+ other assets, mainly for non-U.S. users.
- 🧮 Aave: a DeFi lending protocol where you can borrow against wrapped BTC.
What does a Bitcoin-backed loan cost?
Rates depend on loan size, LTV and provider, and they change often. As of October 2026, published rates start at about 5.8% at Coinbase. SALT advertises 7.49% to 10.5% APR, while Ledn's rates run from 11.49% APR on loans below $250,000 down to 9.25% on loans of $2 million or more. Strike charges between 10.5% and 13% APR on loans with monthly interest payments, and a percentage point more if interest is paid at maturity. Unchained quotes a 12% interest rate, or 14.18% APR. DeFi rates float with supply and demand. Lower LTVs and bigger loans usually get better rates.
Also look for origination fees, prepayment penalties and liquidation fees. These can push the effective cost well above the headline rate.
How to get a Bitcoin-backed loan
- Pick a provider. Compare custody model, rehypothecation policy, rates and where it operates.
- Complete KYC. Centralized lenders require identity verification.
- Choose your LTV and term. A conservative LTV leaves more room before a margin call.
- Deposit BTC into the lender's custody, a multisig vault or a smart contract.
- Receive funds in fiat or stablecoins, then watch your LTV and repay to unlock your Bitcoin.
The future of Bitcoin-backed loans
Bitcoin lending is starting to look like ordinary finance. Regulation is clearer after the GENIUS Act passed in the U.S., and the administration is friendly to crypto, although the broader CLARITY Act stalled in the Senate in September 2026. SVB notes that several major financial institutions launched Bitcoin-backed lending for select clients in the first half of 2026.
Expect more bank participation, more rated securitizations like Ledn's, and more consumer products such as credit cards and longer-term loans. The core risk won't change, though: if Bitcoin's price drops sharply, borrowers who are overextended get liquidated.
DeFi borrowers face added risks, too. In April 2026, after attackers drained $291 million from infrastructure linked to the Kelp DAO project, users of lending protocol Aave struggled to withdraw funds as $6.2 billion flowed out. Borrow conservatively, and know exactly who is holding your coins.

articles.title: Standard Chartered Signs Agreement to Acquire Zodia Custody
articles.text:
Standard Chartered signs definitive deal to acquire Zodia Custody
The signing follows shareholders’ acceptance of Standard Chartered’s non-binding offer in May, with regulatory approvals still pending.
Standard Chartered signed definitive agreements to acquire Zodia Custody’s regulated operating entities, subject to regulatory approvals and closing conditions.
The signing advances a transaction announced in May, when Zodia’s shareholders accepted the bank’s non-binding offer.
As part of the deal, Standard Chartered would acquire 100% of Zodia Custody UK Limited, the parent company of Zodia’s regulated operating entities in Singapore, Hong Kong, Australia, Luxembourg and the United Arab Emirates, the bank said in a Wednesday announcement.
The transaction would integrate Zodia’s crypto custody business into Standard Chartered’s existing Securities Services operations. Zodia would also transfer its software and professional-services assets to Zodia Solutions, an independent entity under SC Ventures, which would provide digital asset infrastructure for financial institutions.
The UK-based lender reportedly began considering folding Zodia’s crypto custody business into its corporate and investment banking division in April.
The acquisition forms part of the lender’s broader expansion in crypto services. In September, Standard Chartered launched spot Bitcoin and Ether trading for institutional clients in the United Arab Emirates.
Related: Standard Chartered wavers on $100K Bitcoin year-end call, says it may be ‘too low’

articles.title: PHP Panic: Two Critical Bugs Put 70% of the Internet at Risk, and Everyone Is Freaking Out - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- PHP released versions 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35 on October 21 to fix CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, two flaws rated 9.2 out of 10 that allow unauthenticated remote code execution.
- Finland, the Netherlands, and France took government websites offline as a precaution after details leaked early and Cloudflare reported attacks hours before the fix shipped.
- Regular users have nothing to install; the fix falls on website owners and hosting companies, and PHP 8.1 and older get no official release.
If you’ve been online at all today, you’ve seen the panic: a critical vulnerability is threatening to “pwn” just about every website on the planet.
Finland just started unplugging government websites on Wednesday, the NSA is recommending all organizations using PHP to shut down their sites, and the Netherlands and France did the same. And no, it wasn't a cyberwar.
The culprit was PHP, a programming language most people have never heard of. You've almost certainly used it today, though: it runs about 70% of all websites whose server-side language is known, according to W3Techs.
PHP is the software working behind the curtain on a website's server—the computer that stores the site and builds each page you ask for. Every WordPress site, for example, sits on a PHP server, per WordPress security firm Wordfence.
Oh, by the way, Wordfence is also down.
Two newly found bugs in PHP itself let a stranger run their own commands on that server without ever logging in. Security people call this unauthenticated remote code execution. Everyone else can call it "someone else is driving now."
If that server stores your account, your address, or your order history, well, that's theirs too. Web host GoDaddy warned the flaws could let attackers steal data, deface sites, or take over servers entirely.
“A flaw like this could let an attacker run their own code on an affected server over the internet, which can lead to stolen data, a defaced site, or a full takeover,” Godaddy says.
What PHP announced
The PHP Foundation, the nonprofit that funds the language's development, raised the alarm on Tuesday. In a statement shared on X, it said: "The PHP security team is giving advance notice: Upcoming security release Wed, Oct 21st 2026, 14:00UTC, two critical vulnerabilities, both rated CVSSv4 9.2. PHP users are encouraged to prepare to update. Earlier release if details become public or active exploit evidence."
The PHP security team is giving advance notice: Upcoming security release Wed, Oct 21st 2026, 14:00UTC, two critical vulnerabilities, both rated CVSSv4 9.2.
PHP users are encouraged to prepare to update. Earlier release if details become public or active exploit evidence.
— The PHP Foundation (@ThePHPF) October 20, 2026
That 9.2 comes from CVSS, the Common Vulnerability Scoring System, which grades how dangerous a bug is based on things like how easily it can be reached over the internet and how much damage it can do. It runs from 0 to 10, and anything from 9.0 up is labeled critical—so these two are about as bad as it gets without hitting a perfect 10.
The fix landed at roughly 13:35 UTC on Wednesday, a few minutes early, as PHP versions 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. The security advisory didn't bother being subtle: "All PHP users are strongly encouraged to update immediately."
But releasing a fix and having everybody implement the solution are not the same thing, so caution is advised.
How the bugs work
The first bug, CVE-2026-109618, shows up when PHP runs out of memory halfway through handling a request, then later treats that half-built data as if it were finished. The second, CVE-2026-109619, lets leftovers from one visitor's request linger in memory after they should have been tossed, where the next request can trip over them.
Think of a cook who keeps reading orders from tickets that are already in the trash. Slip a fake ticket into the bin, and the cook makes whatever you wrote on it. In this case, the “order” is the attacker’s code, and the server runs it.
PHP said the risk is highest on servers using a common Apache setup called mod_php, where a demonstrated exploit works "before any application code runs." In other words, the website's own defenses, like login screens and WordPress security plugins, never even wake up.
PHP foundation researchers pointed at PHP's upload-progress feature, the thing that tracks how much of a file you've sent, as one of the confirmed ways in. It has been switched on by default for more than a decade, and few websites actually use it.
A leak, then attacks
None of this was supposed to be public yet. On Tuesday, someone posted on the Hacker News forum that two PHP flaws would be disclosed that Thursday, while admitting they had "no evidence beyond 'source: trust me, bro.'"
Turns out bro was right. Security firm watchTowr confirmed the bugs were real and under embargo—an agreement to keep details quiet until a fix is ready—and PHP moved its release up a day.
"We are seeing early attacks emerging and are updating mitigations as new vectors show up," Cloudflare CTO Dane Knecht wrote on X early Wednesday morning, nearly six hours before the patch shipped. Cloudflare pushed emergency firewall rules, filters that block known attack patterns, to every customer, but Knecht called them "a stopgap only."
PHP sites behind Cloudflare already have an initial set of WAF rules deployed for the known exploit vectors in these vulnerabilities. The rules are available to all customers, including free.
We are seeing early attacks emerging and are updating mitigations as new vectors show… https://t.co/wMz9tDTWwH
— Dane Knecht 🦭 (@dok2001) October 21, 2026
Governments hit the off switch
Finland's state IT center, Valtori, began taking public web services offline as a precaution, public broadcaster Yle reported, while the Dutch national cybersecurity agency took down its own website.
France's Interior Ministry said its prefecture websites were "temporarily taken offline pending the release of a security patch by the framework's publisher."
CERT-EU, the EU's cyber emergency team, told organizations that couldn't patch to "consider isolating internet-facing applications from public networks until a fix is available." That's bureaucrat-speak for "unplug it." Agencies in Australia, Japan, and the U.K. said much the same, according to Reuters.
What the viral posts got wrong
Viral threads on X claimed PHP versions "dating back to 2004" were vulnerable. That traces back to early estimates that everything since PHP 5 was affected, which CERT-EU admitted is based on social media posts.
E-commerce security firm Sansec puts the range at PHP 5.4 and later. So 2012, not 2004—still plenty old.
PHP only ships official releases for versions 8.2 and newer, which makes the "no fix for old versions" claim half right. Given how bad this one is, its security team also published bare-bones source-code patches for 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1, and Linux distributions are backporting fixes of their own.
Security firm Mallory counted about 884,000 internet-facing hosts advertising PHP 8.1 or older on October 20, or 59% of the roughly 1.5 million that publicly show a version. A single shared-hosting server can carry many websites, so the number of sites behind them is higher.
Some threads also lumped in Node.js, a different web technology that happened to schedule its own, unrelated security update for the same day. Bad timing.
Even patched versions won't reach every server at once. "If you rely on the volunteer maintained https://rpms.remirepo.net we urge you to move to distro packages or building from source now, so you can immediately apply updates. The repo will not have updates today," the PHP Foundation said in its statement, referring to a popular volunteer-run source of PHP packages for Red Hat-style Linux servers.
Should you really care?
You shouldn’t panic, but also shouldn’t shrug it off. A hacked website, for example, doesn't need to touch a blockchain to empty your wallet. In 2024, attackers redirected the front ends of DeFi protocols Compound and Celer to pages that drained connected wallets, and Curve Finance suffered a similar attack in 2025.
I pre-emptively disconnected ALL my sites / VPS servers from the web
I'll wait for the patch to hit at 2 PM UTC
If you have a PHP website, probably good to take them down until you patch PHP
69.3% of the web runs on PHP so this is going to be intense!
Good time maybe to buy… https://t.co/xTXvLwuzrH
— @levelsio (@levelsio) October 21, 2026
Those were DNS hijacks, not PHP bugs, but the trick is the same: the site looks right, the URL looks right, and the "approve" button sends your tokens somewhere else. A compromised server can serve exactly that kind of page.
Hackers can get very creative, very fast, when it comes to zero-day exploits.
Bugs like these are also getting easier to find, with frontier AI models increasingly used to find software vulnerabilities, and experts told Decrypt in June that many more vulnerabilities could surface as those tools spread.
What happens next, and what to do
Once a patch is public, attackers can compare the old and new code to see exactly what was fixed, and the forensics team at cybersecurity firm Sansec said it expects "mass attacks to start within 15 minutes of the release." When a different PHP flaw went public in June 2024, Akamai experienced exploit attempts against its decoy servers within 24 hours.
So should the average person panic? Not exactly. Your phone, browser, and laptop don't need a PHP patch; the work falls on whoever runs the websites you use.
If you run a site, ask your hosting provider whether PHP has been updated, and don't count on WordPress to do it for you: Wordfence warned that automatic updates won't apply this fix and told site owners to find out who is responsible for updating PHP on their servers. Anyone on 8.1 or older needs to plan an upgrade.
"The only thing I can say is that the only mitigation is patching / upgrading PHP,” PHP core developer Gina Peter Banyard said on Mastodon. “I sadly know too much."
And if you're on PHP 8.2, the fix you just got is one of your last: that version reaches end of life on December 31, 2026, after which it gets no more security patches.

articles.title: PancakeSwap TVL Jumps $380M as Fee Overhaul Goes to Vote
articles.text:
PancakeSwap TVL tops $380M as major fee overhaul heads to vote
PancakeSwap’s proposed fee-sharing overhaul would give liquidity providers 88% of swap fees and cut CAKE emissions by 69%, as BNB Chain’s DeFi activity expands.
Decentralized exchange PancakeSwap’s total value locked (TVL) grew nearly 19% over the past week, adding about $380 million as the protocol moves toward a major overhaul of how it distributes trading fees to liquidity providers.
According to DefiLlama, PancakeSwap’s TVL climbed to $2.4 billion on Wednesday, up from about $2.02 billion on Oct. 14. The increase was concentrated in its V3 liquidity pools, where TVL more than doubled to about $739 million from $336 million over the same period.
The growth coincided with PancakeSwap opening a governance vote on a proposal called “The Flip,” which would increase liquidity providers’ share of swap fees on V3 and Infinity pools to 88%, up from 66%-68% on most pools.
The proposal would also gradually reduce daily CAKE token emissions by approximately 69%, from 22,500 to 7,000 tokens. Voting opened on Wednesday, Oct. 21, and will run until Oct. 24, with implementation expected to begin in November if approved.
PancakeSwap leads BNB Chain trading as tokenized stocks expand
PancakeSwap accounted for approximately $4.67 billion in decentralized exchange trading volume on BNB Chain over the past seven days, representing about 71% of the network’s total, according to DeFiLlama. The network also hosts most of PancakeSwap’s liquidity, accounting for roughly $2.33 billion of its $2.40 billion in TVL.
The activity comes amid broader growth across BNB Chain’s DeFi ecosystem. That network’s TVL climbed approximately 8.3% over the past seven days to $5.84 billion, according to DeFiLlama. Decentralized exchange trading volume also surged 40.2% to $6.54 billion over the same period, even as its stablecoin market capitalization declined 0.6% to $13.1 billion.
Related: Curve Finance accuses PancakeSwap of copying its code
Beyond crypto, BNB Chain has also seen an expansion in tokenized equities, a market in which PancakeSwap has an established presence. The decentralized exchange began supporting Binance’s bStocks in June, allowing users to trade tokenized US stocks onchain.
On Oct. 15, Binance announced that bStocks surpassed $1 billion in assets under management, approximately four months after launching. The company reported more than $40 billion in cumulative trading volume and said 11.2% of bStocks’ value was deployed in DeFi in early October.

articles.title: Solana Alpenglow Goes Live in 'Most Ambitious' Upgrade Since Ethereum's Merge - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- Solana's new Alpenglow consensus protocol has gone live on mainnet-beta, replacing TowerBFT at slot 459,653,000, core developer Anza said.
- Transactions now become irreversible in about 150 milliseconds, down from 12.8 seconds, which Anza says matters for exchanges, banks and merchants.
- Further upgrades, including a post-quantum version called Quantumglow, are planned but have no committed dates.
Solana's largest consensus upgrade since the network launched in 2020 went live on Wednesday, cutting the time it takes for a transaction to become irreversible from about 12.8 seconds to roughly 150 milliseconds, core engineering team Anza said.
Validators retired TowerBFT, the consensus protocol Solana had used since March 2020, at slot 459,653,000 at around 14:00 UTC. They switched systems on the running network while carrying its existing ledger forward, with independent operators coordinating a shared handoff point.
The change is to finality, the point at which a transaction can no longer be reversed and the moment an exchange, bank or merchant waits for before treating an asset as moved. Under TowerBFT, Solana gave a conditional confirmation within seconds but took about 12.8 seconds to reach full finality. Alpenglow condenses those two steps into one.
"This is the largest, most ambitious blockchain upgrade since 'The Merge' and Anza took it from a white paper to running on mainnet in under 18 months," said Anza CEO Brennan Watt, referring to Ethereum's 2022 switch to proof of stake.
Before reaching mainnet, Alpenglow went through public testing, including red teaming, penetration testing, repeated migration rehearsals and a security competition, followed by launches on Solana's testnet and devnet. Anza implemented the protocol in Agave, the validator software it maintains, and independent validators activated it.
Anza's research team, led by ETH Zurich professor Roger Wattenhofer with Quentin Kniep and Kobi Sliwinski, published the Alpenglow design in May 2025.
Under Alpenglow, validators send their votes directly to each other instead of writing them into later blocks, and votes are weighted by stake. "If you have 80% of the votes say yes, then it's immediately done," Wattenhofer, Anza's head of research, said in an interview with Solana Foundation technology vice president Jacob Creech published last month. "You immediately know that the block is final."
A second route, two rounds of voting that each need 60% of stake, can be even quicker for validators clustered close together, such as in Europe, he explained. The protocol is designed to keep working with less than 20% of stake acting maliciously and a further 20% offline. If the network goes 10 seconds without finalizing a block, validators gradually lengthen block times until messages get through. "Eventually, even a bad internet will give us a block again," Wattenhofer said.
More upgrades are planned. Rotor will change how block data spreads across the network, and geographically aware leader rotation aims to cut delays as block production passes between validators. Quantumglow, a research design, would swap Alpenglow's elliptic-curve cryptography for hash-based signatures to make it secure against quantum computers while keeping the same finality speed. None has a committed date.
Alpenglow's road to mainnet
Validators approved the upgrade in September 2025, voting 98% in favor of SIMD-0236, the proposal that implements it. "The biggest difference users will feel right away will be a reduction in confirmation latency to approximately 150-200ms," Anza lead economist Max Resnick told Decrypt at the time.
Alpenglow went live on Solana's community test cluster in May 2026, when Resnick said the team was targeting a mainnet activation in late Q3 or early Q4. On October 13, Anza confirmed the October 21 date.
The upgrade also opens the door to other changes. Developers at Jump Crypto's Firedancer team have proposed scrapping Solana's cap of 60 million compute units per block once Alpenglow is live, letting blocks grow as large as the fastest validators can handle while slower ones use its "skip vote" feature to abstain. Critics warned the change could favor well-funded operators and increase centralization.

articles.title: France Proposes Crypto Exchange Liability for DeFi Access
articles.text:
France proposes liability for crypto exchanges offering DeFi access
French authorities want crypto exchanges to conduct checks on DeFi protocols and face liability for certain customer losses under proposed changes to EU crypto rules.
France wants cryptocurrency platforms to face liability for certain decentralized finance (DeFi) incidents if they fail to vet protocols or ignore known security risks.
French authorities published proposals Wednesday to revise the European Union’s Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA). The joint response to a European Commission consultation came from France’s Treasury, the Financial Markets Authority (AMF), the central bank and the Prudential Supervision and Resolution Authority (ACPR).
“CASPs [crypto-asset service providers] should be liable for certain incidents affecting clients where they actively facilitated access,” French authorities said.
MiCA excludes crypto services provided in a fully decentralized manner without intermediaries. France’s proposal would extend investor safeguards by imposing new duties on regulated platforms that connect customers to DeFi protocols.
The Commission is reviewing whether MiCA needs updating as crypto markets develop. Its consultation sought views on activities outside the law’s original scope, including DeFi. The responses will inform a report to EU lawmakers due by June 30, 2027, which could include proposals to amend the law.
DeFi access could come with new obligations
French authorities proposed requiring platforms to vet DeFi protocols before offering access and monitor them for vulnerabilities and suspicious activity. They also backed certification of protocols and smart contracts, along with platform liability for certain incidents.
The requirements would apply fully to significant CASPs, with obligations scaled for smaller providers.
Platforms could still connect customers to uncertified protocols if they conduct their own due diligence and provide enhanced risk disclosures, the authorities said.
Related: Ledger’s early implant warnings deserved more action, Karpelès says
The authorities also addressed non-custodial or self-custodial wallets by opposing blanket certification requirements for developers. They favored voluntary certification for more advanced wallets that integrate DeFi services.
France pushes for wider MiCA overhaul
Beyond DeFi, France backed plans to transfer supervision of “significant CASPs” from national regulators to the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA).
The authorities also proposed lowering MiCA’s current threshold of 15 million average daily active users in the EU for identifying significant CASPs. They also suggested considering custody assets, business risks and group complexity when deciding which platforms should fall under ESMA supervision.
Related: France advances stablecoin tax, eyes self-custodial wallets and exit tax proposals
France also called for a review of MiCA’s asset-referenced token (ART) category, which covers tokens designed to maintain a stable value by referencing assets or combinations of assets. The authorities noted that no ARTs had been authorized under MiCA and proposed adapting the e-money token (EMT) framework to cover multicurrency stablecoins.
Magazine: MiCA is coming for DeFi vaults, but regulation will be difficult

This theory is corroborated by leaked gameplay of an apparent mission, released more than a week ago by notorious Rockstar hacker "Cyberleek." According to the GTA wiki, Lucia is asked to parachute as a stunt to attract investment to the Dacity Coin.
"Give them a show. They'll buy Dacity Coin before they even know what it is," someone tells Lucia on the phone during the mission, according to a leaked screenshot.
In the official launch trailer, a wing walker sets off a smoke bomb atop a plane plastered in Dacity Coin branding. This has led some traders to believe that the Dacity Coin could be featured in multiple missions, with the player tasked with performing crazy stunts to pump the token—just like real-world meme coin traders have done in the past.
Dacity Coin also appears to be connected to an in-game brand called AudaCity, with AudaCity featuring in both the leak and trailer alongside the coin. It appears that AudaCity is the company behind the Dacity Coin, per the GTA wiki.
Some traders believe that the meme coin will feature more heavily than just a couple of side missions. Nicstho said that the bull thesis is that Dacity Coin is an in-game currency that can be spent both in single-player and multiplayer, adding that would be "huge" for the real-world Solana token—despite there being no official link between the two.
"I guess you’ll be able to trade it like you trade stocks on GTA V," pseudonymous meme coin trader Corey Ape told Decrypt. "Just think the last GTA you could buy any of the stocks from the mission on the game, you can probably do the same here."
Corey Ape said that this is purely gut instinct, but it makes sense. In GTA V's single-player story mode, gamers could invest in stocks in an attempt to get rich quick—entire investment guides were created around this feature. Corey Ape believes it is only natural for an in-game meme coin to be tradable by gamers, after Rockstar set this precedent in the last game.
"Obviously the [real-world] coin hasn't been launched by Rockstar," Nicstho said. "They just want to mog memecoin traders."
As rumours and speculation continue to swirl, the real-world Solana token has soared. One trader has unrealized profits of $285,000 from just a $20,000 investment, according to trading platform Pump.fun. Though it's important to stress none of this is realized and it could sharply fall at any moment, as is the nature of meme coins.
A section of crypto traders are now eagerly awaiting GTA 6's November release, hoping it'll pump their bags.
Rockstar did not respond to Decrypt's request for comment.

articles.title: Bitcoin Price Faces $87,700 Resistance From Late 2025 Buyers: Glassnode
articles.text:
Bitcoin ‘top buyers’ halt BTC price upside with $87.7K now key: Glassnode
Bitcoin price current resistance near $87,000 was reinforced by investors who bought BTC in late 2025, per new research.
Bitcoin (BTC) investors sitting on unrealized losses are capping price gains at $87,700, while ETF inflows strengthen support at $80,000, analysis reveals.
Key points:
- Bitcoin investors who bought BTC in the latter stages of 2025 have an aggregate cost basis of around $87,700, which now functions as resistance per Glassnode analysis.
- The area immediately above $87,000 hosts several resistance levels including the 2026 open at $87,490 and the 20-month moving average at $87,165.
- Bitcoin price support at $80,000 strengthens as bid liquidity focuses on this psychological level.
Bitcoin 2025 buyers add to $87,000 resistance zone
New research from onchain analytics platform Glassnode reveals that the breakeven point for a cohort of new Bitcoin holders is currently acting as resistance.
Since the start of the year, two groups of holders have kept BTC/USD from moving higher once it challenges their acquisition cost basis.
In November 2025, price lost the cost basis of investors with entries between six and 12 months prior, which sat at $94,000 at the time. When price attempted to break above the trendline at $97,100 in January 2026, it became resistance, triggering a rejection and sending price lower.
A similar resistance trendline is given by the cost basis of investors who bought BTC one to two years prior. This cohort slipped into aggregate loss in February of this year as price lost its cost basis of $76,900. In May, the cost basis halted a price rebound at just above $82,000.
In both cases, underwater buyers looking to exit their positions at breakeven produced a wall of sell-side pressure that new demand could not match. Commenting, Glassnode noted the extent of BTC price retracements after rejections from either cost basis.
“Bitcoin rose to the 6-12 month cost basis in January and then fell by more than a third. It met the 1-2 year cost basis in May and fell by about a quarter,” it said. “The 1-2 year holders also stepped up their selling into the rally at the start of October.”
The cost bases for the six-to-12-month cohort and one-to-two-year cohort are currently $87,700 and $99,500, respectively.
BTC/USD chart with cohort breakeven levels (screenshot). Source: Glassnode
The area above $87,000 also contains the 2026 opening price at $87,490 and the 20-month simple moving average (SMA) for BTC/USD at $87,165, a level that has historically preceded new all-time highs once reclaimed as support.
ETF cost basis hosts new BTC price support
Below current spot price, the cost basis of the US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs) marks one of several support levels of interest around the $80,000 mark.
Related: XRP 30-day exchange inflows pass 6B tokens as whales move to the sidelines
Glassnode calculates the spot ETF cost basis at $81,500, while Bitcoin’s true market mean — the cost basis for all BTC acquired on secondary markets — sits at $77,500. Below this, the breakeven point of Bitcoin’s short-term holders — wallet entities holding a given amount of BTC for up to six months without selling — lies at $74,600.
As an important psychological level, $80,000 now forms a magnet for bid liquidity across exchange order books.
“The block sits just under the US Spot ETF Cost Basis, so the zone between $80K and $81.5K is where order-book and on-chain support overlap. A break below it would bring the liquidation cluster just under $80K, and then the True Market Mean near $78K, into play,” Glassnode commented.
BTC/USD chart with cost-basis data, true market mean (screenshot). Source: Glassnode

articles.title: Morning Minute: Bitcoin Tops JPMorgan’s Ten-Year Forecast for All Assets - Decrypt
articles.text:
GM!

- Crypto majors are green up led by ZEC +13%; BTC at $83.5k

Bitcoin Tops JPMorgan’s Ten-Year Forecast for All Assets
JPMorgan Asset Management just released its 2027 Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions, the 31st edition of a report institutional allocators build their models around. It contains thirteen asset classes, ranked by expected compound return over the next decade.
Bitcoin is at the top of it.
JPMorgan projects a whopping 10% annually for Bitcoin over 10 to 15 years. REITs come second at 8.2%, small caps 7.7%, U.S. large caps 7.5%. Gold lands at 5.5%. Over a decade of compounding, $100 in Bitcoin becomes $259 against $206 in large caps and $171 in gold.
This is the first time Bitcoin has appeared in the report at all, and that matters more than the number. Pension consultants and RIAs run their allocation models off assumptions like these, and for the past thirty editions Bitcoin’s expected return was undefined. Now it has a figure, from JPMorgan, at the top of the table.
Bitcoin’s arithmetic return is 20.9% while the compound figure is 10%, a 10.9-point gap that is pure volatility drag. For large caps that same gap is 1.45 points. Annualized volatility: 55%, against 18% for stocks. The forecast isn’t that Bitcoin is a better version of stocks. It’s that Bitcoin pays more and makes you live through considerably more to collect it. Anyone who has lived through the ups and downs of crypto cycles over the past decade would agree.
Two things stand out for crypto. The debasement argument just lost its loudest potential endorsement. JPMorgan called that bull case “wide of the mark” and put gold near the bottom of the table. And Bitcoin is no longer being measured against gold at all. It’s being measured against REITs and small caps, the growth sleeve of a normal portfolio, and winning.
The timing is pointed too. The 10-year Treasury yields above 5% and JPMorgan’s global bond forecasts are the highest in two decades, and the bank still put Bitcoin on top.
A 10% compound return won’t make anyone rich on a Twitter timeline. But it’s now the highest number in JPMorgan’s book. The institutions that needed permission to model Bitcoin just got it. Now we wait for the market to catch up.

articles.title: Shinhan Card, SBI Plan Yen Stablecoin Tests for Japan–Korea Travel
articles.text:
Shinhan, SBI make Japan-Korea tourist spending a test case for yen stablecoins
The companies will assess safeguards for travelers and whether stablecoins can speed up trade settlement between South Korea and Japan.
South Korea’s Shinhan Card announced Wednesday that it signed an agreement with Japan’s SBI VC Trade and SBI XDC Network APAC to test yen stablecoin payments for travelers and cross-border trade settlement.
Under the pact signed Tuesday, the companies will test stablecoin card payments, wallet-to-wallet payments and cross-border trade settlement. They will also assess anti-money-laundering and fraud-detection controls.
Shinhan Card is one of South Korea’s biggest credit card companies. SBI is a Japanese financial heavyweight that runs banks, brokerages, insurers and crypto exchanges.
The latest initiative is intended to support cross-border payments and settlement between the East Asian nations and improve payment convenience for travelers.
Travel between the two countries generated more than 10 million visitor arrivals in the first eight months of 2026, according to official tourism figures from both countries. South Korea was Japan’s largest source of foreign visitors with 7.42 million arrivals. Japan was its neighbor’s second-largest source with 2.7 million arrivals.
Shinhan Card announced in April that it had completed a proof-of-concept testing that covered stablecoin payments and cross-border settlement.
SBI VC Trade registered in March 2025 as Japan’s first electronic payment instruments exchange service provider, enabling it to handle USDC.

articles.title: OCC Finalizes GENIUS Act Stablecoin Rules Ahead of January Deadline - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- The OCC finalized its rule implementing the GENIUS Act, setting standards for stablecoin issuers under its jurisdiction before the law takes effect on January 18, 2027.
- The rule covers reserves, redemption, risk management, custody and capital, but leaves anti-money laundering and sanctions rules to a separate rulemaking with Treasury.
- The banking regulator said it will announce separately when it starts accepting applications and waiver requests from prospective stablecoin issuers.
The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency issued its final rule implementing the GENIUS Act on Wednesday, setting out the requirements that stablecoin issuers under its oversight will have to meet when the law takes effect on January 18, 2027, the banking regulator announced.
The rule applies to payment stablecoin issuers that fall under the OCC's jurisdiction, including subsidiaries of national banks and federal savings associations, nonbank issuers approved at the federal level and some state-qualified issuers, as well as foreign issuers and certain custody activities at OCC-supervised firms, according to an OCC bulletin.
.@USComptroller Jonathan V. Gould: Today’s final rule advances @POTUS Trump’s and @SecScottBessent’s vision for American leadership in digital assets. We are providing a clear, practical framework for payment stablecoin innovation, with strong standards for reserve backing,… pic.twitter.com/k1vfHYLUMQ
— OCC (@USOCC) October 21, 2026
Most of the requirements sit in a new section of the OCC's regulations covering reserve assets, redemption, risk management, audits and reporting, custody, applications, the supervision of foreign issuers, and a capital and operational backstop. The rule also covers how state-qualified issuers transition to the federal framework, and when the OCC can revoke an issuer's approval.
Rules on the Bank Secrecy Act, anti-money laundering and sanctions are not included, and will come in a separate rulemaking with the Treasury Department.
"We are providing a clear, practical framework for payment stablecoin innovation, with strong standards for reserve backing, redemption, and risk management," said Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan Gould.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent compared the GENIUS Act to Abraham Lincoln's National Currency Act of 1863, which "established a national framework for bank-issued currency."
The OCC received hundreds of comments on its proposal from crypto companies, community bankers, trade groups and academics, among others. Given "the nascency of the industry," the agency said it would monitor how the sector develops and adjust its framework where necessary.
The road to GENIUS rules
Signed into law in July 2025, the GENIUS Act bars anyone other than a permitted issuer from issuing a payment stablecoin in the U.S., and stops digital asset service providers from offering or selling stablecoins to Americans unless they come from a permitted issuer or a foreign issuer that meets certain requirements.
The OCC proposed its rules in February, opening a 60-day comment period. The proposal also left out anti-money laundering and sanctions rules, which Treasury's FinCEN and OFAC proposed separately in April, requiring issuers to run anti-money laundering programs, report suspicious activity and maintain sanctions compliance programs.
Regulators missed the law's earlier July deadline for finalizing their rules. In August, Gould said the OCC was "very intent on moving quickly and getting a final rule out by November so that we will be able to start processing applications within the new year."

articles.title: Zcash Rallies 12% as NU7 Mainnet Upgrade Nears
articles.text:
Zcash rallies 12% as developers finalize NU7 activation height
Zcash extended triple-digit year-to-date gains as developers agreed on the NU7 mainnet activation height, targeting Nov. 5, with node synchronization work still pending.
Zcash (ZEC) surged about 12% over the past 24 hours, as developers agreed on a mainnet activation block for the network’s NU7 upgrade, expected in early November.
The token traded around $1,270 at last look on Wednesday, according to CoinGecko. The rally coincided with a Tuesday GitHub proposal by Zcash developer Sean Bowe setting the activation at block 3,543,405, expected around Nov. 5.
The value of the privacy-focused cryptocurrency that uses advanced trustless zero-knowledge proofs is up more than 148% year to date.
“Height agreed at ZIP editor meeting,” Bowe wrote, adding that the team still needed to finalize the upgrade specifications before merging the proposal. Two developers approved the changes.
The Zakura NU7 dashboard also lists the upgrade as pending on mainnet at block 3,543,405, with activation expected around Nov. 5.
NU7 aims to reduce Zcash’s target block time by two-thirds to 25 seconds, allowing transactions to receive confirmations more quickly. The upgrade from 75-second block time has been undergoing testing since early October.
Meanwhile, the Zcash Foundation’s NU7 readiness tracker showed six of 12 tasks completed, with remaining work involving Zebra node synchronization issues and mainnet preparations. Developers have not confirmed whether these outstanding issues could affect the planned activation date.
Related: Zcash activates NU7 on testnet ahead of November mainnet target

articles.title: 'Mentality Issue': PlayStation Founder Waves Away Disc Ownership Anger - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- Ken Kutaragi, the founder of PlayStation, said that physical discs are a "metaphor" for owning games, and calls it a "mentality issue" if you're upset about physical discs not being produced.
- It follows Sony's decision to discontinue the production of game discs as of 2028, which has received major backlash from fans.
- Game veterans told Decrypt that the disc decision is usually pushed by publishers to boost profits, and that Sony miscalculated its community's reaction.
PlayStation founder Ken Kutaragi has pushed back against fans' anger over Sony's plan to discontinue physical game discs, calling it a "mentality issue." One game industry veteran claims that cutting discs is "only" ever pushed by publishers as they seek better profit margins.
It comes amid a storm of controversy surrounding Sony's decision to stop disc production in 2028. Former PlayStation exec Shawn Layden called it a "heavily spreadsheeted decision" and said it damaged the company's reputation. Meanwhile, fans have garnered more than 385,000 signatures on a "Don't Kill the Disc" petition.
"I understand that physical discs have become a metaphor for 'owning' games. I really understand that mentality," Kutaragi said at the Game Republic New Horizons event. "But nobody thinks [physical media] is necessary for a networked device like a smartphone, for example, because people feel that they will keep their content. So it's a mentality."
Kutaragi retired from PlayStation in 2007 and is best known for being the architect of the first three generations of the PlayStation console. Since leaving, two more generations of the console have been released. He is currently serving as CEO of Japanese companies Ascent Robotics and Cyber AI Entertainment.
“I really understand [why some people are upset]," he said, according to the Video Games Chronicle. "But I don’t think it’s economically reasonable. Maybe it’s a mentality issue.”
Former creative strategist for Infinity Ward Robert Bowling told Decrypt that publishers are the "only ones ever pushing" to cut physical game discs. He said that it is because cutting discs can increase profit margins by reducing the cost of production, as well as crushing the game reseller market led by the likes of GameStop.
"It speaks to the divide that has formed in our industry between those who see games as just a software product," Bowling, who is now studio head for game studio //18.bravo, told Decrypt, "And those who see them as something more like art, entertainment, collectibles, and a lifestyle."
Sony has argued in court that no reasonable consumer believes that they own digital games they buy on the PlayStation Store, according to court filings. Instead, Sony says that Store purchases equate to purchasing a revocable license.
Game industry veteran Chris Heatherly said that corporate executives are used to "issuing decrees" from their offices and "hiding behind their PR teams," but that doesn't work in the social media age. He argues that Sony isn't "in dialogue" with its audience, so it misjudged how the move would land.
"I think it’s insult upon injury for gamers who feel used and abused by these console makers in general," Heatherly told Decrypt. "If you look at Steam, people buy way more games than they play because they like to collect games. What is that other than owning them? You’re not playing them at all!"
That said, Heatherly argues that it isn't "an entirely rational coherent thought process" to want to own online multiplayer games, since the publisher usually controls the servers anyway. But he thinks there is a middle ground.
"I think there are models for ownership worth talking about, but not fake financialized ownership like web3," he told Decrypt. "I think people would be happy with local forever and peer-to-peer [online services], frankly."

articles.title: Drift Exploiter Sends $109M in ETH to Tornado Cash in 2 Days
articles.text:
Drift exploiter sends $109M in Ether to Tornado Cash in 2 days
Wallets linked to the $295 million April hack still held $138 million in Ether after sending another $46 million to the mixer Wednesday.
A Drift exploiter-linked wallet transferred 18,800 Ether, worth about $46 million, to Tornado Cash on Wednesday.
The exploiter transferred $61 million in Ether to the crypto mixer on Tuesday, taking its two-day total to 44,510 ETH, or $109 million, as blockchain data tracker Onchain Lens said on X.
The transfers to Tornado Cash make the funds harder to trace and represent nearly 37% of the $295 million stolen from decentralized exchange (DEX) Drift in April. The attack ranks as this year’s third-largest crypto hack, according to DefiLlama.
The Drift exploiter-labelled wallets still held 56,569 Ether, worth roughly $138 million after Wednesday’s flurry of transfers, Arkham data shows.
The Solana-based DEX reported about $295 million in losses from the April 1 hack, which its security consultant Mandiant attributed to a North Korean threat group.
Drift opened claims and redemptions for DFX recovery tokens on Oct. 1, giving affected users a claim on a pool that launched with about $3.1 million and receives exchange revenue and recovered funds.
Related: HEX token sellers erase $160M following reports of Richard Heart’s arrest

articles.title: Irish drug lord's lost Bitcoin fortune comes back to life as $41 million moves to Coinbase
articles.text:
Quick Take
- A wallet linked to Irish drug dealer Clifton Collins moved another 500 BTC worth $41 million after nearly 11 years of inactivity.
- The transfer brings Collins-linked Bitcoin movements to 2,500 BTC worth $208 million, reviving a fortune once thought lost in a landfill.
- Another 3,500 BTC worth $291 million remains, while questions persist over who controls the funds and whether further recoveries are possible.
A Bitcoin wallet linked to convicted Irish drug dealer Clifton Collins moved about $41.5 million after a decade of inactivity.
Blockchain analytics firm Arkham Intelligence reported that 500 BTC moved on Oct. 20 from an address associated with Collins to a wallet it identifies as a Coinbase Prime deposit.
The transfer marks the fifth movement of 500 BTC from Collins-linked wallets this year, bringing the total to 2,500 BTC, worth approximately $208 million at Bitcoin's price of around $83,157.
The development leaves roughly 3,500 BTC, valued at $291 million, in wallets Arkham associates with the former drug dealer, raising questions about whether the remaining fortune could also become accessible.
The October transaction follows the same pattern seen in July and August, when separate wallets transferred 500 BTC each to the same Coinbase Prime-linked address.
Blockchain records show that the latest transfer originated from coins received in January 2016, meaning those specific holdings had remained unspent for nearly 11 years.
The receiving address subsequently redistributed the funds across 42 outputs, including 40 transfers of exactly 10 BTC. Similar distributions followed the earlier movements, suggesting a recurring process for handling the Bitcoin.
However, the transactions do not show whether any assets were sold or identify who authorized the latest transfer.
Irish authorities' Bitcoin recovery raises questions over remaining $291 million
Collins, a former security guard and cannabis cultivator, accumulated approximately 6,000 BTC between 2011 and 2012 using proceeds from drug dealing.
He reportedly split the holdings into 12 wallets with 500 BTC each and stored the private keys needed to access them on printed paper hidden inside a fishing rod case.
Following his imprisonment in 2017, his landlord reportedly disposed of his belongings, including the case, at a landfill in County Galway.
The incident left the Bitcoin widely presumed inaccessible for years, until Irish authorities began recovering portions of the fortune earlier in 2026.
In March, Ireland's Criminal Assets Bureau (CAB), working with Europol's European Cybercrime Center, announced it had accessed a wallet containing 500 BTC, then worth about €30 million.
The bureau subsequently announced another 500 BTC recovery in May, followed by a third seizure in July, bringing its officially confirmed total to 1,500 BTC.
Europol provided investigators with technical expertise and decryption resources, though authorities have not publicly explained how they recovered access to the previously inaccessible wallets.
Another 500 BTC moved in August before October's latest transaction, extending the series of transfers beyond the amounts detailed in the bureau's July confirmation.
Arkham considers law enforcement the most likely party behind the movements, citing their recurring size and similarities to earlier confirmed seizures. However, Irish authorities have not publicly established their role in the latest transaction.
The transfers to Coinbase Prime also introduce uncertainty over the eventual disposition of the recovered assets.
Coinbase's institutional platform provides custody and trading services, allowing large Bitcoin holdings to be transferred without necessarily being sold on the open market.
Ireland's Criminal Assets Bureau handles the sale or disposal of seized property on a case-by-case basis under applicable court orders.
The bureau has not yet disclosed whether it will retain or liquidate the latest 500 BTC, while the remaining 3,500 BTC could represent another substantial recovery if authorities gain control of the associated wallets.

articles.title: UK Banks Hit With 10,000 Complaints Over Blocked Crypto Transfers in 90 Days: Report - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- Advocacy group Stand With Crypto said UK bank customers filed 10,092 complaints over blocked or restricted transfers to crypto exchanges in 90 days.
- Lloyds Banking Group received 2,297 complaints, followed by Barclays with 1,569 and NatWest Group with 1,278, according to the report.
- The group urged the FCA and Treasury to make clear that sector-wide blocks are not proportionate, ahead of the UK's crypto regime taking effect next year.
UK bank customers sent 10,092 complaints about blocked or restricted transfers to crypto exchanges over 90 days, crypto advocacy group Stand With Crypto said in a report published on Tuesday.
The complaints were filed by 9,803 people between May and August 2026 through an online tool run by the group, and concerned transfers to platforms registered with the Financial Conduct Authority, the UK's financial regulator. They came from every one of the UK's 650 parliamentary constituencies, the group said in a tweet.
📣 We are pleased to announce our report, Blocked: Britain’s Crypto Access Problem, is live.
In just 90 days, people sent 10,092 complaints to their banks about fiat transfers to crypto exchanges being blocked or restricted. Complaints came from every single one of the UK’s 650… pic.twitter.com/jWXbhbJTyZ
— Stand With Crypto In The UK🛡️🇬🇧 (@StandWCrypto_UK) October 20, 2026
Lloyds Banking Group, which includes Halifax and Bank of Scotland, received the most, with 2,297, or more than 22% of the total, even though it has no published policy restricting crypto transfers. Barclays received 1,569 and NatWest Group, which includes Royal Bank of Scotland, 1,278. HSBC UK also received more than 1,000, according to the report, which does not give its exact total. Virgin Money and the Co-operative Bank received the fewest, with 103 and 76 respectively. Decrypt has reached out to Lloyds Banking Group and HSBC UK for comment.
Six banks publish limits on crypto transfers, according to the report. Barclays caps them at £2,500 per transaction and £10,000 every 30 days, NatWest at £1,000 a day and £5,000 every 30 days, and Santander UK at £1,000 per transaction and £3,000 every 30 days. Starling, TSB, Chase UK, Metro Bank, Virgin Money and the Co-operative Bank block crypto transfers entirely.
"The protection of our customers' funds is our highest priority," a Barclays spokesperson told Decrypt. "Like many other banks, we've introduced limits on payments to cryptocurrency exchanges to help protect customers from crypto-related scams and losses."
A spokesperson for NatWest referred to a statement on the bank's website, which highlights a "growing risk from fraudsters," exploiting the popularity of cryptocurrency. "To help protect our customers and keep their money safe and secure, we took the decision to block or limit online banking, debit card transactions and mobile app Faster Payments identified as going to cryptocurrency exchanges from 16th March 2023," the bank said.
Banks that apply limits received 6,198 complaints, while those with no published policy, Lloyds and Revolut, received 2,842. Banks with outright bans received 989, which the report suggests may be because their customers know not to try.
"A customer cannot reliably use their bank's published policy to predict whether they will be able to transfer their own money to a crypto asset platform," the report said.
The figures are not weighted by each bank's market share, since the number of current accounts each offers is not public, and customers could complain to more than one bank.
The UK's crypto regime
The report cites a 2025 FCA and YouGov survey in which 13% of UK crypto users said they had faced problems withdrawing crypto to their bank account, the most common negative experience reported. Its findings also echo a January survey by the UK Cryptoasset Business Council, which estimated that banks were blocking or delaying around 40% of transfers to the country's 10 largest exchanges, with one exchange seeing close to £1 billion in declined transactions over a year.
Some restrictions date back years. TSB has banned crypto purchases since 2021, and Barclays blocked crypto purchases made with its credit cards from June 2025. Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has pledged to outlaw banks from denying services to customers over their involvement with crypto if he becomes prime minister.
Lawmakers have also taken up the issue, though their focus has largely been on crypto businesses rather than individual customers. Parliament's Crypto and Digital Assets All-Party Parliamentary Group launched an inquiry in July into crypto firms' access to bank accounts and services, which also covers the transfer limits and payment blocks banks impose. In August, its co-chairs, Labour MP Gurinder Singh Josan and Lord Vaizey of Didcot, wrote to the chief executives of every major UK bank asking how they treat crypto firms and what limits they apply to crypto-related transactions. Access to banking services "could be one of the single biggest barriers to growth" for UK crypto businesses, they warned.
Stand With Crypto called on banks to replace blanket restrictions with risk-based, case-by-case checks, to publish plain-language policies on when crypto transfers may be blocked, and to give customers a way to challenge or opt out of controls on transfers to FCA-registered providers.
It also urged the FCA and HM Treasury to state publicly that sector-wide blocks and hard caps on transfers to registered or authorized crypto firms are unlikely to be justified by anti-fraud or financial crime rules. The FCA's crypto regime comes into force next year, and firms that have secured authorization "should have assurance" they will not face blanket barriers from other regulated firms, the report said.
