articles.title: NASA vô tình phát hiện căn cứ quân sự bí mật dưới lớp băng dày tại Greenland
articles.text:
Trong chuyến bay gần đây qua dải băng Greenland, nhà khoa học Chad Greene của NASA vô tình phát hiện một căn cứ quân sự bí mật.
Sau khi chụp ảnh radar khu vực này, Greene rất ngạc nhiên với điều ông phát hiện ra, nơi sau đó được xác nhận là Trại Century, một căn cứ quân sự của Mỹ thời Chiến tranh Lạnh được xây dựng từ 65 năm trước ở độ sâu 30m dưới dải băng khổng lồ.
"Chúng tôi đang tìm kiếm nền băng và Trại Century xuất hiện. Lúc đầu, chúng tôi không biết đó là gì", Alex Gardner, một nhà khoa học về tầng băng tại Phòng thí nghiệm Động cơ phản lực (JPL) của NASA, người đã chỉ đạo dự án cho biết.
Lối vào Trại Century. (Ảnh tư liệu).
Được quân đội Mỹ xây dựng bí mật từ tháng 6/1959 – 10/1960, Trại Century, còn được gọi là "thành phố dưới băng", bao gồm 21 đường hầm ngầm dài gần 3.000m.
Greene cho biết các hình ảnh radar cho thấy căn cứ có nhiều cấu trúc riêng biệt.
Để nghiên cứu căn cứ này, NASA đã sử dụng radar khẩu độ tổng hợp gắn trên máy bay không người lái (UAVSAR), tương tự công nghệ LiDAR được dùng để tìm kiếm khu phế tích Maya. Điểm khác biệt là LiDAR sử dụng ánh sáng laser, còn UAVSAR dùng sóng vô tuyến.
Mỹ và Đan Mạch ký thỏa thuận phòng thủ Greenland vào năm 1951 để cho phép các thành viên của Tổ chức Hiệp ước Bắc Đại Tây Dương (NATO) sử dụng cơ sở tại Greenland để bảo vệ vùng đất này và các thành viên khác của liên minh.
Thỏa thuận này cho phép Mỹ xây dựng các căn cứ tại Greenland. Với mức nhiệt -70 độ C và gió thổi hơn 200km/giờ, việc xây dựng một căn cứ dưới trên thềm băng trở thành nhiệm vụ cực kỳ khó khăn. Khu trại này được xây dựng từ 6.000 tấn vật liệu, được vận chuyển bằng xe trượt tuyết hạng nặng chỉ có thể di chuyển với tốc độ tối đa 3km/giờ.
Vật liệu được chuyển bằng xe trượt tuyết đến Thule, một căn cứ khác của Mỹ, và mỗi chuyến như vậy kéo dài 70 giờ đồng hồ. Lực lượng kỹ sư quân đội đầu tiên đào các chiến hào trong tuyết và băng trước khi làm các tòa nhà bằng gỗ có mái thép.
Căn cứ này có 1 lò phản ứng hạt nhân PM-2.
Trại Century không phải là một bí mật. Quân đội Mỹ thậm chí đã làm video quảng bá dự án này. Nhưng khám phá mới của NASA có ý nghĩa quan trọng về mặt chiến lược hạt nhân mà cả Chính phủ Đan Mạch cũng không biết.
Được gọi là "Dự án Iceworm", Trại Century được chuẩn bị để chứa tên lửa đạn đạo dưới lớp băng Greenland. Kế hoạch của Mỹ là làm thêm hơn 130.000km2, đủ để chứa 600 tên lửa. Mỹ cũng cần xây dựng 60 bệ phóng và đưa 11.000 binh lính đến sống trong thành phố dưới băng.
Tuy nhiên, Dự án Iceworm không bao giờ thành hiện thực vì thiếu khả thi. Đến năm 1967, Trại Century ngừng hoạt động và bị bỏ hoang, trở thành tàn tích lạnh lẽo của những nỗ lực Chiến tranh Lạnh của Mỹ. Giờ đây, căn cứ bỏ hoang bị chôn vùi dưới nhiều băng tuyết hơn trong 57 năm qua.

articles.title: Scientists who discovered a third form of magnetism win major physics prize
articles.text:
Scientists who discovered a third form of magnetism win major physics prize
Physicists have discovered a third form of magnetism hidden for over a century, potentially rewriting physics textbooks and transforming future technology.
- Date:
- October 18, 2026
- Source:
- Johannes Gutenberg Universitaet Mainz
- Summary:
- Physicists have uncovered a hidden third form of magnetism that challenges more than 100 years of established physics. Called altermagnetism, the discovery could transform future computing and electronics while opening an entirely new frontier in quantum research.
- Share:
Scientists have uncovered a previously unknown form of magnetism, overturning an understanding of magnetic behavior that had stood for more than a century. The discovery, known as altermagnetism, has revealed a third fundamental category of collinear magnetism and opened new possibilities for quantum materials, advanced electronics, and future computing technologies.
Three physicists responsible for the breakthrough have been named recipients of the 2026 Europhysics Prize, one of Europe's most prestigious honors in condensed matter physics. The European Physical Society (EPS) Condensed Matter Division selected Professor Jairo Sinova of Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz (JGU), Dr. Libor Šmejkal, and Professor Tomas Jungwirth for their work establishing altermagnetism as a distinct form of magnetic order alongside ferromagnetism and antiferromagnetism.
"This award recognizes a fundamental discovery that challenged one of the most established paradigms in condensed matter physics," said Professor Jairo Sinova, Director of the Spin Phenomena Interdisciplinary Center (SPICE) at Mainz University. "Discovering that an entirely new magnetic phase had remained hidden for more than one hundred years demonstrates that even the most mature scientific fields can still hold fundamental surprises."
The breakthrough emerged from years of collaboration between Sinova's research group at Mainz University and Jungwirth's team at the Institute of Physics of the Czech Academy of Sciences in Prague. Šmejkal, who also maintained an affiliation in Prague, spent eight years at Mainz between 2016 and 2024, first pursuing doctoral research and later working as a postdoctoral scientist in Sinova's group.
During that period, Šmejkal played a leading role in developing the theoretical framework behind altermagnetism. By combining advanced mathematical approaches to symmetry with spintronics, which studies how electron spin can be used in electronic devices, the researchers identified a previously unrecognized pattern of magnetic behavior.
Their predictions soon attracted experimental teams around the world. Measurements of electronic properties and electrical transport in multiple materials provided evidence supporting the new magnetic classification. Altermagnetism has since grown into one of the most active areas of condensed matter physics, with research efforts expanding across Europe, North America, and Asia.
A Third Form of Magnetism Rewrites Physics
For more than 100 years, physicists generally divided collinear magnets into two fundamental categories: ferromagnets and antiferromagnets.
Ferromagnets have an overall magnetic alignment that produces a net magnetization. These materials are essential to many magnetic memory technologies used today. In conventional antiferromagnets, opposing magnetic moments cancel one another, leaving no overall magnetization and producing electronic behavior very different from that of ferromagnets.
Altermagnetism introduces a surprising third possibility.
Like antiferromagnets, altermagnets have magnetic moments that cancel out, resulting in no net magnetization. However, their electrons can exhibit properties previously associated with ferromagnets.
This unusual combination allows altermagnets to support electrical currents with strongly polarized electron spins while also displaying extremely rapid magnetic dynamics. Those characteristics could make them valuable for a new generation of spintronic devices, potentially advancing the speed and capabilities of future information technologies.
The significance extends well beyond electronics. Altermagnetism represents a previously unrecognized symmetry class of matter and has revealed unexpected connections to several major areas of modern physics, including topological phenomena, unconventional superconductivity, and quantum materials with strong interactions between electrons.
How Scientists Discovered Altermagnetism
The path toward this discovery began with theoretical investigations into unusual ways that electricity moves through magnetic materials. Among the early advances was the prediction of the crystal anomalous Hall effect, a phenomenon involving electrical transport in certain crystal structures.
Initially, these unexpected behaviors might have appeared to be unusual features of individual materials. However, the researchers eventually recognized that they were connected by a broader principle involving symmetries of electron spins.
Rather than representing isolated exceptions to established magnetic behavior, these materials belonged to an entirely different magnetic category.
A major milestone came in 2022, when the team published a comprehensive symmetry classification of altermagnetism and identified hundreds of materials that could potentially exhibit it.
Experimental physicists subsequently tested these predictions using several complementary methods. These included angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES), which reveals how electrons behave inside materials, along with measurements of electrical transport.
The results confirmed altermagnetic behavior in several materials, helping establish the new classification experimentally.
Interest in the discovery has expanded rapidly. Hundreds of scientific papers have appeared within just a few years, and altermagnetism has become a prominent subject at international physics conferences. The growing research community is now investigating both its fundamental properties and its potential technological applications.
Discovery Earns Prestigious 2026 Europhysics Prize
The Europhysics Prize recognizes major advances in condensed matter physics, a field concerned with the physical properties and behavior of materials. Established in 1975, the award honors discoveries that have significantly advanced scientific understanding, with a substantial share of the recognized research conducted in Europe.
The 2026 prize recognizes the theoretical and experimental advances that established altermagnetism as a new fundamental form of collinear magnetic order.
The award ceremony was scheduled for September 2026 at the 32nd General Conference of the European Physical Society Condensed Matter Division (CMD32) in Graz, Austria.
The Scientists Behind the Breakthrough
Professor Jairo Sinova is a physics professor at Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz in Germany and director of the university's Spin Phenomena Interdisciplinary Center. His research investigates magnetism, spintronics, and quantum materials.
Dr. Libor Šmejkal conducted much of the crucial theoretical work that led to the identification of altermagnetism while working at Mainz University from 2016 to 2024. His current affiliations include the Max Planck Institute for the Physics of Complex Systems, the Max Planck Institute for Chemical Physics of Solids, and the Institute of Physics of the Czech Academy of Sciences.
Professor Tomas Jungwirth is affiliated with the Institute of Physics of the Czech Academy of Sciences and the University of Nottingham. He has collaborated extensively with Sinova's Mainz research team and played a central role in establishing the theoretical foundations of altermagnetism.
Together, their work has revealed a fundamental property of magnetic matter that escaped recognition for more than a century, opening an entirely new direction for research into quantum physics and future electronic technologies.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Johannes Gutenberg Universitaet Mainz. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

articles.title: Uranium from World War II reveals how close the Nazis were to an atomic bomb
articles.text:
Uranium from World War II reveals how close the Nazis were to an atomic bomb
A new look at the uranium and heavy water used by the Nazis reveals whether they were close to making a reactor for an atomic bomb.
The Nazis were far from completing a working reactor for their atomic bomb program, despite claims by the project's leader that it was almost ready, a new study finds.
The German physicist Werner Heisenberg wrote in 1947 that the reactor for the "Nazi bomb" project — which culminated in Germany's B8 nuclear reactor — was almost finished at the end of World War II.
Heisenberg, who led the reactor's development, claimed the reactor was "just insufficient" to create a self-sustaining fission reaction and that it lacked only a "relatively small amount of uranium" to work.
If it had worked, the B8 reactor would have confirmed that a fission chain reaction was possible, marking a key step toward the German development of an atomic bomb. It could have also spurred the development of specialized fission reactors used to create weapons-grade plutonium from uranium. Instead, the atomic bomb was developed first by the United States and was used to force the surrender of Japan in August 1945. (Germany had already surrendered in May 1945.)
The new study, published Sept. 29 in the journal PNAS Nexus, used historical documents and forensic investigations of two of the project's surviving uranium cubes to refute Heisenberg's claim. The new research indicates that the German B8 reactor had less than half the amount of "heavy water" and about half the amount of uranium it would have needed for a continuous chain reaction.
"My results argue that Heisenberg was off by roughly a factor of two," said first author Patrick Park, a doctoral student at Princeton University who co-wrote the study while at Columbia University.
Park said Heisenberg's mistake was understandable: His calculations were only approximate, and the project was relocated to a rock cellar in the town of Haigerloch, Germany, after Berlin was bombed.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.
"People were dying or starving and so these reactor calculations were not his first priority," while many details of neutron physics were unknown at that time, Park told Live Science in an email. "Given these circumstances, I think he did the best he could."
Heavy water
To answer the question of how far the reactor for the Nazi bomb project got, the scientists began by tracing archival records of hundreds of uranium cubes that had been used by German scientists. The B8 reactor consisted of five concentric circles of uranium cubes suspended on chains within the heavy water tank. The German scientists planned to place a radium-beryllium neutron source into the reactor's core to kick-start the chain reaction with a flood of neutrons that would split the uranium nuclei and release more neutrons, furthering the chain reaction.
Heavy water is a form of water that contains the neutron-heavy hydrogen isotope deuterium. Like the mainly-graphite blocks and rods used in many reactors, it can be used to "moderate" or slow down fast neutrons created in a fission reaction so they trigger fission — and more neutrons — in nearby uranium atoms. The Germans also used small amounts of graphite in their reactor, but as a coating to reflect neutrons back into the chamber.
By combining the records of the cubes, heavy water and graphite used by the German scientists with measurements of the two surviving cubes, the study authors created a mathematical model of the reactor that agreed closely with historical measurements. This enabled them to establish that the heavy water reactor was far from achieving a stable reaction. The findings also helped them examine the suggestion that the Germans should have instead built a graphite-based reactor like the nuclear pile developed at the University of Chicago to build the American bomb.
But the study authors determined that a graphite-moderated reactor was unfeasible in wartime Germany because the local supply of coal available to create graphite contained high levels of neutron-absorbing boron, making it useless.
Instead, the heavy water used in the B8 reactor was produced at a single factory in Norway, which was occupied by Germany from April 1940 until May 1945. However, the reactor contained only about 370 gallons (1,400 liters) of heavy water, instead of the more than 780 gallons (roughly 3,000 liters) it would have needed, the researchers determined.
Heavy water makes up a tiny fraction of a percent of ordinary water, and extracting it by electrolysis in the Norwegian factory took extraordinary effort. The factory was producing as much heavy water as it could, but the B8 reactor would have needed more than twice the amount it produced during the entire war, the researchers wrote.
Another finding is that the B8 reactor had about half the amount of uranium it would have needed to sustain a fission chain reaction. The reactor contained a total of 664 cubes, each weighing about 5.11 pounds (2.32 kilograms), for a total of 3,390 pounds (1,540 kilograms) of uranium. Similar cubes were distributed among other experimental groups, giving a total inventory in wartime Germany of about 1,100 cubes of uranium.
But the researchers determined that the B8 reactor would have needed at least 1,200 cubes to work. Germany, therefore, was not about to develop a reactor for an atomic bomb in 1945. Contrary to Heisenberg's claims, the heavy-water reactor was not nearly ready, and a working graphite reactor was impossible.
"We conclude Germany could not have built heavy water nor graphite reactors during World War II," the researchers wrote.
Related stories
Mark Walker, a historian at Union College in Schenectady, New York, who wasn't involved in the study, said the findings explain Germany's decision to develop a heavy-water reactor, since a graphite reactor was not feasible and they didn't know at the time how much heavy water would be needed.
Walker is the author of "Hitler's Atomic Bomb: History, Legend, and the Twin Legacies of Auschwitz and Hiroshima" (Cambridge University Press, 2024) and a noted expert on Germany's wartime nuclear efforts. He agreed that Germany could not have made a graphite reactor during World War II.
"This paper argues that if the Germans had done something they did not do, then this would have failed," he told Live Science in an email. "While this is counterfactual history, it is an interesting engineering analysis."
Park, P. J., Robertson, B., Hiebert, M. E., Zhao, J., Sivels, C. B., & Koeth, T. W. (2026). Nuclear archaeology reassesses Heisenberg’s last reactor experiment. PNAS Nexus, 5(9). https://doi.org/10.1093/pnasnexus/pgag282
Tom Metcalfe is a freelance journalist and regular Live Science contributor who is based in London in the United Kingdom. Tom writes mainly about science, space, archaeology, the Earth and the oceans. He has also written for the BBC, NBC News, National Geographic, Scientific American, Air & Space, and many others.

articles.title: Scientists tested 39 sweeteners and uncovered surprising gut effects
articles.text:
Scientists tested 39 sweeteners and uncovered surprising gut effects
- Date:
- October 17, 2026
- Source:
- University of Cambridge
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered that many common sweeteners can interfere with gut bacteria, with some combinations involving medications producing surprisingly strong effects. One sweetener mixed with a widely prescribed antidepressant reduced beneficial bacteria and microbial diversity in laboratory experiments, raising new questions about potential effects on gut health and immunity.
- Share:
Common sweeteners may be doing much more inside our bodies than simply replacing sugar. Scientists at the University of Cambridge have discovered that many widely used sweeteners can directly interfere with the growth of gut bacteria, and their effects can become even more pronounced when combined with medications or other everyday substances.
In laboratory experiments involving 39 sweeteners and 25 species of gut bacteria, researchers found that roughly three-quarters of the sweeteners altered the growth of at least one bacterial species. Some slowed or completely stopped the growth of microbes associated with a healthy digestive system.
One combination stood out in particular. When the sweetener isosteviol was paired with the antidepressant duloxetine, it strongly suppressed two important gut bacteria involved in maintaining digestive health and regulating blood sugar. The combination also disrupted the balance of a simulated gut microbiome and produced changes that could have implications for inflammation and immune responses.
The findings, published in Molecular Systems Biology, raise new questions about how sugar substitutes interact with the body. However, the researchers emphasize that their experiments were conducted in the laboratory, not in humans, and further studies are needed to determine whether these effects have real-world health consequences.
Are Artificial Sweeteners Really Harmless to Gut Bacteria?
Sweeteners have become a familiar ingredient in modern diets. They appear in everything from soft drinks and candy to desserts, packaged snacks, and breakfast cereals, often providing sweetness with fewer calories than traditional sugar.
These ingredients are frequently promoted as healthier alternatives to sugar. Yet growing research has identified associations between sweetener consumption and health conditions such as type 2 diabetes, obesity, and cancer. Such associations do not necessarily mean that sweeteners cause these diseases, and scientists are still working to understand the biological mechanisms that might explain the findings.
One area of particular interest is the gut microbiome, the enormous collection of bacteria and other microorganisms that inhabit the digestive tract. These microscopic residents help break down food, produce useful compounds, support the immune system, and contribute to metabolic health.
Although sweeteners are consumed around the world, surprisingly little research has directly examined how they affect individual gut bacteria. Most previous investigations have relied on animal experiments or studies comparing dietary habits and health outcomes across large groups of people.
Professor Kiran Patil from the Medical Research Council (MRC) Toxicology Unit at the University of Cambridge said: "Most of what we know about the potential impact of sweeteners on our health comes from animal research or from population studies. While these studies have indicated involvement of the microbiome in mediating the effect of sweeteners, it's difficult to know how sweeteners act in the body - is it through direct interactions with our gut bacteria?"
An additional challenge is that people rarely consume sweeteners on their own. They are typically mixed with other ingredients, and those combinations may change how they behave.
"Answering this is further complicated by the fact that we rarely ever take sweeteners by themselves - we take them with drinks, in snacks, or even in medication to mask bitterness," added Dr. Sonja Blasche, a lead author of the study, also the MRC Toxicology Unit.
Scientists Put 39 Sweeteners to the Test
To investigate these interactions, Blasche and her colleagues designed a series of laboratory experiments examining both artificial and naturally derived low-calorie sweeteners.
The team cultivated 25 different species of gut bacteria, including microorganisms considered beneficial, neutral, or potentially harmful. Each species was grown separately so researchers could measure how it responded to specific sweeteners without interference from other bacteria.
They then exposed these bacterial cultures to 39 commercially available sweeteners and monitored whether the microorganisms continued multiplying normally.
The results revealed a surprisingly widespread effect. Approximately three out of every four sweeteners changed the growth of at least one bacterial species.
In some cases, bacterial populations grew more slowly. In others, growth stopped entirely. Several affected species are associated with maintaining a healthy gut environment, suggesting that certain sweeteners can directly influence microorganisms that contribute to digestive health.
However, the effects were not uniform. Different sweeteners influenced different bacteria, showing that these substances cannot necessarily be treated as a single group when evaluating their biological activity.
More Than 100 Unexpected Interactions With Everyday Substances
The researchers then explored a question that previous studies had largely overlooked: What happens when sweeteners are combined with other ingredients or medications?
To find out, they tested sweeteners alongside several commonly encountered substances, including caffeine, vanillin (vanilla extract), advantame (an artificial sweetener), and eight widely used drugs.
The combinations produced more than 100 instances in which a sweetener's effect on bacterial growth changed in the presence of another substance.
In 34 cases, the combinations intensified the effects on bacteria. In another 68 cases, the effects became weaker.
These findings suggest that the way a sweetener influences gut microbes may depend not only on the sweetener itself but also on what accompanies it.
A compound that has a relatively modest effect when tested alone could behave differently when combined with an ingredient in a beverage, a food additive, or a medication.
A Sweetener and Antidepressant Combination Stands Out
Among all the combinations investigated, one produced especially striking results.
The researchers found that isosteviol, a sweetener used in the food and beverage industry, strongly inhibited two important gut bacteria when paired with the antidepressant duloxetine.
The affected species were Roseburia intestinalis and Parabacteroides merdae, both associated with important functions in the digestive system, including processes related to gut health and blood sugar regulation.
Duloxetine is a widely prescribed medication. In the United States alone, more than 4.2 million patients received prescriptions for the drug in 2023.
The laboratory findings suggest that certain sweeteners and medications can interact in ways that substantially alter the growth of particular gut microbes.
However, this does not establish that people taking duloxetine experience these effects or that consuming isosteviol alongside the medication is harmful. Understanding whether the same interactions occur in the human body will require additional research.
The Combination Also Disrupted Gut Microbiome Diversity
Studying individual bacterial species provided valuable information, but the human gut is far more complicated than a collection of isolated microbes.
Inside the digestive system, bacteria coexist in large, interconnected communities. Different species compete for nutrients, exchange chemical compounds, and influence one another's growth.
To better approximate this environment, the researchers created a simplified artificial gut community containing all 25 bacterial species from their initial experiments.
After allowing the community to develop, they introduced different combinations of sweeteners and drugs. They then tracked changes in bacterial populations and measured the overall diversity of the microbial community.
Microbial diversity refers to the variety of microorganisms present and how they are distributed within a community. A diverse gut microbiome is generally considered important for maintaining digestive health and supporting the stability of the intestinal environment.
The results showed that combining isosteviol with duloxetine reduced bacterial diversity and changed the relative abundance of different species.
In other words, the combination did more than affect a few bacteria individually. It altered the makeup of the broader microbial community.
Additional experiments revealed another potentially important effect. The bacterial community exposed to the isosteviol and duloxetine combination showed increased toxicity toward certain host cells and altered the behavior of other cells involved in inflammation and immune responses.
These observations suggest that interactions between sweeteners, medications, and gut bacteria could have consequences beyond bacterial growth alone, although whether similar effects occur in people remains unknown.
Scientists Challenge a Common Assumption About Sweeteners
The results raise questions about the widespread assumption that low-calorie sweeteners have little direct biological activity.
A substance described as metabolically neutral is generally understood to have limited effects on the body's metabolic processes. The new experiments suggest that, at least under laboratory conditions, some sweeteners can interact directly with gut microorganisms.
Dr. Blasche said: "Sweeteners are often marketed as metabolically neutral, but our study challenges this idea. We found that they can directly affect gut bacteria, particularly when mixed with other compounds such as medication and food additives. These common combinations could have unintended effects on our gut microbiome."
The findings also highlight why examining individual food ingredients in isolation may not provide a complete picture of how they behave.
A typical meal or beverage contains multiple compounds, and people may also be taking medications that interact with those substances. The Cambridge experiments demonstrate that such combinations can sometimes produce substantially different effects than the ingredients do separately.
What Does This Mean for Human Health?
Despite the striking results, the scientists caution against drawing immediate conclusions about the safety of sweeteners or their interactions with prescription medications.
All experiments were carried out in controlled laboratory settings using isolated bacterial cultures or simplified microbial communities. The human digestive system contains a much larger and more complex population of microorganisms, along with many additional biological factors that could influence the outcome.
It remains unclear whether the changes observed in the laboratory would occur under normal dietary conditions or whether they would translate into measurable health effects.
Nevertheless, the research provides a foundation for investigating how common sweeteners, food additives, and medications might interact inside the digestive system.
Professor Patil, the study's senior author, added: "Our study suggests that artificial sweeteners don't just pass through the body passively -- they can interact with gut microbes, and these effects can be amplified or altered by other substances like medications. These findings can help guide new studies towards understanding how sweeteners might influence health in unexpected ways."
Rather than establishing that sweeteners are harmful, the findings point to an important area of research that has received relatively little attention: how everyday combinations of food ingredients and medications may influence the microscopic communities that help keep us healthy.
The research was funded by the European Union's Horizon 2020 program and the UK Medical Research Council.

Common xenobiotics modulate gut microbial responses to low‑calorie sweeteners in vitro. Molecular Systems Biology, 2026; 22 (9): 1453 DOI: 10.1038/s44320-026-00225-6

articles.title: Tại sao núi lửa dưới biển không bị nước biển dập tắt?
articles.text:
Chúng ta đều biết được rằng nước có thể dập tắt được lửa, không ở đâu nhiều nước bằng đại dương. Thế nhưng tại sao nước ở đó vẫn không thể dập tắt được núi lửa?
Khi nghĩ về núi lửa, nhiều người có thể sẽ tưởng tượng ra một ngọn núi hình nón cao chót vót đang tỏa ra một cột khói dày đặc, trông giống như một ngọn núi đang phun trào. Hơn nữa sau khi núi lửa phun trào, một lượng lớn tro núi lửa màu trắng sẽ rơi xuống cả một vùng rộng lớn. Vì vậy, nhiều người trong tiềm thức nghĩ rằng núi lửa thực sự có thể phun trào ra lửa.
Núi lửa phun trào.
Nhưng nếu chúng ta quan sát cận cảnh các ngọn núi lửa, thì hoàn toàn không phải vậy. Bởi vì dung nham (magma) do núi lửa phun trào thực chất là một chất lỏng có nhiệt độ cao, về bản chất, nó hoàn toàn khác với lửa.
Những bức ảnh chụp cận cảnh dung nham cho thấy rõ ràng rằng chúng là chất lỏng. Khi chúng ta học vật lý từ hồi còn đi học, chúng ta sẽ biết sự biến đổi của ba pha vật chất: Khí, lỏng và rắn liên quan đến điểm nóng chảy và điểm sôi.
Dung nham (magma) do núi lửa phun trào thực chất là một chất lỏng có nhiệt độ cao
Lấy nước làm ví dụ, nhiệt độ nóng chảy của nước là 0 độ C và nhiệt độ sôi là 100 độ C. Khi nhiệt độ thấp hơn 0 độ C, chúng ta thấy nước rắn - nước đá; khi nhiệt độ nằm trong khoảng giữa 0 độ C và 100 độ C, chúng ta thấy nước ở dạng lỏng; khi nhiệt độ cao hơn 100 độ C, nước sẽ ở thể khí - hơi nước.
Về cơ bản, tất cả các chất đều như vậy, có điểm nóng chảy và điểm sôi, và thay đổi trạng thái pha theo nhiệt độ. Magma là đá nóng chảy do thành phần đá phức tạp, nhiệt độ nóng chảy và sôi của các thành phần khác nhau bên trong không đồng nhất nên hầu hết magma thực chất là hỗn hợp rắn, lỏng và khí. Ngược lại, ngọn lửa xuất hiện khi núi lửa phun trào là một quá trình các chất dễ cháy giải phóng ánh sáng và nhiệt. Trong ngọn lửa này, các thành phần vật chất chính là carbon dioxide, hơi nước, oxy, nitơ và các loại khí khác.
Thứ mà núi lửa phun trào là magma.
Sau khi hiểu rằng thứ mà núi lửa phun trào là magma, và magma là vật thể nóng chảy ở nhiệt độ cao chứ không phải lửa, bạn sẽ có thể hiểu rằng khi núi lửa ngầm phun trào, magma xâm nhập vào nước biển thực chất giống như để một cái vòi liên tục phun nước nóng vào bể chứa nước lạnh - nước lạnh làm mát nước nóng, nhưng không làm nước nóng biến mất theo cách giống như nước dập lửa. Bởi vậy nước biển không thể dập tắt được những ngọn núi lửa ngầm dưới biển.
Bởi vì núi lửa là sản phẩm của sự lưu thông nhiệt và vật chất cấp hành tinh nên những ngọn núi lửa này vẫn liên tục hoạt động. Toàn bộ Trái đất thực ra đều vận hành theo những quy luật cơ bản của vật lý và hóa học. Những quy luật này chúng ta đều đã được học ở trường trung học.
Ví dụ, sự hình thành và hoạt động của núi lửa có thể được giải thích bằng định luật thứ hai của nhiệt động lực học - nghe có vẻ rất chuyên nghiệp, nhưng nó lại rất gần gũi với cuộc sống của chúng ta: Nhiệt luôn tự phát từ nguồn nhiệt có nhiệt độ cao đến nguồn nhiệt có nhiệt độ thấp.
Nếu lần ngược lại lịch sử tiến hóa của Trái đất trong 4,6 tỷ năm, chúng ta sẽ thấy tác dụng của quy luật này: Khoảng 4,6 tỷ năm trước, Trái đất dần dần được sinh ra bởi sự va chạm của vô số hành tinh, và năng lượng của sự va chạm đã được chuyển hóa thành nhiệt, khiến Trái đất lúc bấy giờ giống như một quả cầu magma khổng lồ (toàn bộ hoặc phần lớn bề mặt là magma), và nhiệt độ bề mặt của nó cao tới hàng nghìn độ C.
Sau đó, vì magma có thể chảy được, vật liệu nặng sẽ chìm xuống và vật liệu nhẹ nổi lên. Khi vật chất nặng chìm xuống, thế năng hấp dẫn sẽ chuyển hóa thành nhiệt năng; đồng thời, các nguyên tố phóng xạ ban đầu nằm rải rác trong các hành tinh sẽ tập hợp lại với nhau, phân rã liên tục và đồng thời giải phóng năng lượng.
Những năng lượng này giữ cho magma ở bên trong Trái đất luôn ở trạng thái nóng lên. Nhưng đồng thời do nhiệt độ nền của vũ trụ rất thấp, trung bình là -270 độ C nên Trái đất liên tục truyền nhiệt ra bên ngoài dưới dạng bức xạ nhiệt (có 3 cách truyền nhiệt: Dẫn nhiệt, đối lưu nhiệt và bức xạ nhiệt, nhưng vũ trụ là chân không, không có môi trường nên Trái đất chỉ có thể truyền nhiệt ra bên ngoài dưới dạng bức xạ nhiệt). Vì nhiệt được truyền đi nên Trái đất sẽ phải nguội đi, bề mặt Trái đất nguội đi trước, vì vậy magma ở đây sẽ tạo thành đá, chính là lớp vỏ ban đầu.
Trái đất dần dần được sinh ra bởi sự va chạm của vô số hành tinh.
Đến nay, Trái đất đã phát triển theo cấu trúc về cơ bản là có 3 lớp: Vỏ, manti và nhân, nhiệt độ sẽ tăng ngày càng cao khi đi từ vỏ đến nhân. Đồng thời, do vật chất nặng không ngừng chìm xuống nên mật độ của nó ngày càng cao hơn - mật độ trung bình của lớp vỏ là 2,8g/cm3, mật độ trung bình của lớp manti là 4,59g/cm3, mật độ trung bình của của lõi là 11 g/cm3. Vì vậy, chúng ta cũng có thể nghĩ rằng lớp vỏ đang "nổi" trên lớp manti - giống như một tấm ván nổi trên mặt nước.
Do lớp vỏ rất mỏng so với manti và nhân nên độ dày trung bình của vỏ chỉ khoảng 17km (33km đối với vỏ lục địa và 10km đối với vỏ đại dương). Ngược lại, độ dày của lớp manti tới 2.850km. Do đó, sự chuyển động của lớp manti sẽ khiến cho những lớp đá rắn mỏng này bị xé toạc và di chuyển cùng với lớp manti.
Các phần của lớp vỏ Trái đất bị xé nát trở thành các mảng, và khi lớp vỏ Trái đất di chuyển, một số sẽ va chạm vào nhau và một số tách ra khỏi nhau.
Magma có thể chảy được, vật liệu nặng sẽ chìm xuống và vật liệu nhẹ nổi lên.
Theo lẽ thường, có thể biết rằng ranh giới của các mảng tách rời này rất mỏng và dễ vỡ, vật liệu lớp phủ bên dưới chúng có thể dễ dàng phá vỡ sự phong tỏa của lớp đá và bị đẩy ra khỏi bề mặt - ở đây sẽ tạo thành một vành đai núi lửa dài dọc theo các ranh giới mảng.
Và khi các mảng ngày càng cách xa nhau, magma nguội đi sau khi núi lửa phun trào ở ranh giới mảng tạo thành một lớp mỏng, tức là lớp vỏ đại dương - bởi vì nó mỏng hơn nhiều so với lớp bên trong của mảng, nên nó sẽ trũng hơn các khu vực khác, theo thời gian, nước sẽ tích tụ lại tạo thành các đại dương.
Núi lửa ngầm thực chất là kết quả của sự chuyển động của các mảng
Trên thực tế, đại dương được hình thành theo cách này và sự hình thành của đại dương cũng liên quan chặt chẽ đến sự chuyển động của các mảng.
Do đó, núi lửa ngầm thực chất là kết quả của sự chuyển động của các mảng, và hầu hết chúng là ranh giới của sự phân tách mảng. Kể từ Thế chiến II, với việc con người ngày càng đi sâu khám phá đại dương đã giúp cho chúng ta phát hiện ra các vành đai núi lửa ngầm dài, hầu hết nằm ở giữa đại dương, được gọi là các sống núi giữa đại dương. Chúng là những ngọn núi dài nhất thế giới, với tổng chiều dài khoảng 80.000km.

articles.title: 'The Russians were the problem in the end': Sailor Matt Rutherford on being intercepted by the FSB while attempting to circumnavigate the Arctic Ocean solo
articles.text:
'The Russians were the problem in the end': Sailor Matt Rutherford on being intercepted by the FSB while attempting to circumnavigate the Arctic Ocean solo
Live Science spoke with Matt Rutherford, a sailor and founder of the environmental nonprofit Ocean Research Project, about his attempt to circumnavigate the Arctic Ocean and why he'll have to try again next year.
Sailor Matt Rutherford has dreamed for several years of becoming the first person to circumnavigate the Arctic Ocean solo, nonstop and unassisted. He finally set out from western Greenland on June 25 to achieve this goal, but threatening encounters with Russia's security agency less than two months later forced him to reverse course.
Rutherford is the founder and executive director of the nonprofit environmental organization Ocean Research Project, which gathers and analyzes marine data from a sailboat. His route took him around the southern tip of Greenland, through the Denmark Strait and into the Greenland Sea. From there, he sailed through the Norwegian and Barents seas, and reached Russia's Novaya Zemlya archipelago in mid-August.
He was planning to continue to Canada and end his journey where it started, but Russian officials halted him in his tracks and ordered him to turn around.
On his way home, Rutherford told Live Science about his adventures and why he wants to complete this loop. In an interview on Sept. 23, he also revealed what he'll do differently on his next attempt to avoid another Russian interception.
Matt Rutherford is a sailor and the founder of the Ocean Research Project, a nonprofit that conducts marine research from a sailboat. Matt is the first solo sailor to complete a circumnavigation of North and South America nonstop. This achievement in 2011 inspired his new circumnavigation project in the Arctic Ocean.
Sascha Pare: Where are you currently, and what are the conditions like?
Matt Rutherford: I'm about halfway between Greenland and Newfoundland in the Labrador Sea. The conditions aren't too bad; I mean, it's close to a gale, but it's not quite a gale. [Editor's note: A gale is defined as an area of sustained surface winds of 34 to 47 knots (39 to 54 miles per hour).] It's just a little hard to do anything. I've got dishes in the sink that are all wedged in there that I really need to deal with — but I don't feel like it, because you're just getting tossed around. Waves are crashing on the cockpit. Normally, I do video calls under a dodger [a canvas screen on a boat or ship that provides protection from spray], and you can see the ocean in the background… But I'm going to get hit by a wave if I do that.
SP: You're sailing home to Maryland after a rather perilous expedition. How long have you been at sea for?
MR: I left in mid-May, and I've been basically underway for the most part since then. At this time, currently, I've only been at sea for a few days, because I left Greenland a few days ago. The longest stretch I was continuously at sea this year is 59 days, although I was planning on doing longer than that, so that sucked. Essentially, I was attempting to do a nonstop, single-handed circumnavigation of the Arctic. That's where this all sort of came out of. I tried in 2018, but you couldn't get the Russian permits. And the Russians were the problem in the end [this year]. I got defeated by Russian bureaucracy, essentially. And there was some weird stuff going on with the ice up there this year. [Editor's note: Sections of the High Arctic were impassable due to a relatively cold summer and solid ice fields.]
SP: What happened with the Russians that forced you to turn back?
MR: The FSB got me. [Editor's note: The Federal Security Service (FSB) is Russia's main security agency and a successor to the Soviet Union's KGB.] They boarded me twice, actually. I've never been boarded in the ocean in my life, and I've been sailing 20 years, all over the place. I got about 1,000 miles [1,600 kilometers] into Russia, roughly. I got into the Northern Sea Route. If you just draw a line due north, I was due north of West China — it was way over there, about halfway around the world in the Arctic. I made it about halfway, because I started in Aasiaat, Greenland.
They boarded me once, and then they turned me around and boarded me again. It's a bit of a strange situation, I guess. Two days after I turned around, the ice that I was waiting to open opened, and I sent them an email — the NSRA, the Northern Sea Route Association in Moscow — and said, "Hey, it's open. Can I pretty please go?" And they just got mad at me, like, "You'll be in violation of your permit; you have to turn around."
SP: You're planning to try the circumnavigation again next year. Will you do anything differently to make sure you complete it?
MR: The boat's pretty good to go — which is great, because that's a huge time sink. Ideally, hopefully, if I can get north of [the Norwegian archipelago] Svalbard again like I did this year, then I'm going to stay north of [the Russian archipelago] Franz Josef Land, and I'm going to basically ride the polar ice cap all the way from Svalbard to the Northwest Passage — all the way to Alaska and beyond, essentially.
Because I've learned how the FSB operate, and I know where they're keeping their ships now. Even though I was north of Novaya Zemlya, they still were able to get me. But if I'm over there, north of Frank Josef, they don't go that far, so they won't be able to get me up there. I've figured out a couple of other things that I'm not even going to say, honestly — there are workarounds to get them to [leave me alone]. I'm going to go a little bit quiet.
The NSRA gives you the permit to do this, but the FSB are the people who patrol it. And the FSB don't like the NSRA. I learned that when they boarded me, because they think that they're the ones who should control the Northern Sea Route, not the NSRA. So there's [a] beef between them; they don't talk. There's a lack of communication, which benefits me. I can lean heavy onto the NSRA side, because they don't have boats; they're not going to board you. And they're the ones you have to check in with every 24 hours in Moscow; you've got to send them an email every 24 hours. So I'll do all of that stuff with those guys, but I think there's some ways I can avoid the FSB even knowing where I am, essentially, while still complying with my permit in the NSRA.
Basically, I've got to do the Northern Sea Route without getting within 12 miles [19 km] of any Russian land, period — even a little island, even a rock that sticks out that's 10 feet by 10 feet [3 by 3 m]. That's going to be real tricky, because there are a lot of little islands down there. But the FSB is mostly on the European side; they have almost no boats over on the east side or the middle. So if you can get past the European side by hugging the coast way the hell north, hopefully I can get past where they patrol, and then I can just shoot on through.
Nobody else in the world does this — nobody else in the Arctic, nobody else anywhere. There's literally no other body of water on Earth where you've got to get permits, and then you've got to get boarded like this. It's only Russia, and only north of Russia. And that's because there's a huge amount of natural gas, they think, buried above Russia. So Russia's trying to claim everything to the North Pole.
Technically, it's international waters, so the U.N. is like, "No, this is not right." And Russia's like, "Whatcha gonna do about it?" It's kind of hard to argue with that — and it's north of Russia, so nobody else is there. They've got free rein, and they've got all the icebreakers and whatever else.
Everything else is about the same. I need to secure my hot sauce better, because every time I open my cabinet, they fall out all over the place. There's little things like that — quality-of-life things. I'll probably bring some more heated socks — electric socks and electric gloves. I'll try to make better videos — but I'm not a content creator, and I don't want to be an influencer.
SP: Can you tell me a bit about your background and what led you to this point?
MR: I did this whole circumnavigation of the Americas — nonstop, single-handed — back in 2011 where I spent 309 days alone at sea on this little 27-foot (8 meters) boat. When I got back from that big, crazy trip — which I made a documentary about ["Red Dot on the Ocean: The Matt Rutherford Story"] — I created a nonprofit called Ocean Research Project, where, basically, we use sailboats to do research. We focused mostly in 2013 and 2014 on garbage-patch-related microplastics. In 2013, we mapped out the eastern side of the Atlantic garbage patch, because nobody had got to the eastern side of it. I think it was 160,000 pieces per square kilometer, or something like that. And then, we did some stuff in 2014 in the Pacific garbage patch with the University of Tokyo; we did a joint paper with them.
But mostly what we focus on is Arctic research. Since 2015, we've been heading up to Greenland — sometimes the Northwest Passage also, but primarily Greenland — doing research related to glaciers, for the most part. An ocean-terminating glacier sort of has a river of melted water underneath it, and it creates upwelling, and the upwelling has nutrients. So it mixes nutrients with the ocean and creates this perfect recipe for growth for phytoplankton and zooplankton. And then, we look at the different stages of decay between an ocean-terminating glacier, a land-retreated glacier or a deglaciated fjord. In the middle phase, when a glacier starts retreating back on land, it just creates a river of muddy water, essentially; it turns the fjord into a mud puddle. You can't have photosynthesis if you're in a mud puddle.
SP: Have you been collecting samples or data on this expedition?
MR: Well, it's a little tricky on a boat under these circumstances. I took 50 samples, which were just water samples, and those were from Newfoundland to Aasiaat, Greenland. Nicole [Nicole Trenholm, Ocean Research Project's science director] has a NASA internship out at JPL [Jet Propulsion Laboratory]. She was publishing a paper looking at their model that they have [ECCO-Darwin], and I've kind of forced my way into the paper — well, the organization did, with Nicole's help — by adding these samples. Now we have in situ data, physical data, that we can compare to the model data. That was the only thing we did this year. It's a couple-thousand-mile stretch with 50 water samples in it, so it's a pretty straightforward sort of thing.
Nicole is trying to publish multiple peer-reviewed scientific papers from our previous data. She's got a traffic jam of data, so she needed some time to finish publishing papers from stuff we've collected over the last few years. There is no money anyways. I could still grab some samples on the way up there [Greenland]. And it's trying to promote the nonprofit through it, because people will pay a lot more attention to this stuff than they pay to traditional research expeditions.
Exclusive to Live Science Pro
- 'If you do want to be a criminal, there is no better place to do it': Author Rose George dives into the dark depths of the fishing industry
- 'They don't deserve this beauty and this breathtaking fragility': Former Antarctic tour guides told researchers why they quit the troubling industry
- The ozone layer was supposed to be healing. So why is this year's Antarctic ozone hole so big?
SP: What are your hopes for the Ocean Research Project once you tick off this goal?
MR: Basically, we're trying to expand the organization over the next couple of years. I'd like to bring in another one or two more scientists, because we're up there for three months in Greenland, and sometimes we go to the Northwest Passage — and it's a lot for one scientist.
The big problem we're having is that when Elon Musk was part of DOGE [U.S. Department of Government Efficiency], they cut a massive amount of polar funding — something like 88% of it — because apparently climate change is a hoax and they hate it and you're not allowed to research it either, right?
Basically, nobody's got money. We don't typically get NSF [National Science Foundation] funding; we get more foundation funding, because it's hard to get NSF funding, even before all this stuff. Now that the funding has been cut on the governmental level, a lot more scientists are going after the foundation grants that we used to have a lot less competition for. That makes it a little tricky, too, because now they're getting a flood of requests that they didn't usually get in the past.
This interview has been condensed and edited lightly for clarity.
Help us improve Live Science Pro: We're always trying to make our content better. Leave us feedback about Pro here.
Sascha is a U.K.-based staff writer at Live Science. She holds a bachelor’s degree in biology from the University of Southampton in England and a master’s degree in science communication from Imperial College London. Her work has appeared in The Guardian and the health website Zoe. Besides writing, she enjoys playing tennis, bread-making and browsing second-hand shops for hidden gems.

articles.title: Scientists find a youth protein that helps aging brain cells act young again
articles.text:
Scientists find a youth protein that helps aging brain cells act young again
- Date:
- October 17, 2026
- Source:
- The Mount Sinai Hospital / Mount Sinai School of Medicine
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered that a protein linked to youth helps protect the brain’s immune cells from age-related decline. Restoring the protein in older mice improved the cells’ ability to clear debris and reduced signs of inflammation, raising hopes for future treatments targeting brain aging and Alzheimer’s disease.
- Share:
A protein associated with youth may help aging brain cells regain some of their lost abilities. Scientists at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai have discovered that TIMP2 plays an important role in keeping the brain's immune cells healthy, offering new clues about how the brain changes with age.
In a study published in Nature Communications, researchers found that removing TIMP2 caused brain immune cells, known as microglia, to develop characteristics linked to aging and neurodegenerative disease. When the scientists restored TIMP2 in the bloodstream of older mice, these cells became better at removing cellular debris and showed fewer molecular signs of inflammation and other potentially harmful changes.
The discovery suggests that proteins associated with youth may help preserve the brain's natural defenses as it ages. It also identifies TIMP2 as a potentially important factor in maintaining healthy immune activity in the brain.
Why the Brain's Immune Cells Become Less Effective With Age
Getting older is the greatest known risk factor for Alzheimer's disease and other neurodegenerative disorders. However, scientists still do not fully understand the biological processes that make the aging brain increasingly vulnerable to these conditions.
One important piece of the puzzle involves microglia, specialized immune cells that serve as the brain's maintenance and defense system. They remove cellular waste, help maintain the networks through which neurons communicate, and respond when brain tissue is injured.
As the brain ages, these cells can lose some of their ability to perform these essential tasks. They may also shift into states that promote inflammation and interfere with normal brain function.
"TIMP2 facilitates healthy function for the brain's immune cells," said Joseph M. Castellano, PhD, Associate Professor of Neuroscience at the Ronald M. Loeb Center for Alzheimer's Disease and The Friedman Brain Institute at The Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, and corresponding author of the study. "By supporting the ability of microglia to clear debris and limit maladaptive responses, TIMP2 may help restore aspects of microglial function that become compromised with age. Since our previous work identified TIMP2 as a regulator of synaptic plasticity through the extracellular matrix, these findings suggest that this factor sits at the intersection of several processes that are critical for normal brain function."
Synaptic plasticity refers to the brain's ability to strengthen or weaken connections between neurons, a process essential for learning and memory. The extracellular matrix is a network of molecules surrounding cells that helps support and regulate their activity.
What Happens When the Brain Loses TIMP2?
To investigate how TIMP2 affects brain immune cells, the research team studied several groups of mice representing different biological conditions.
The study included Brittany Hemmer, PhD, the first author, who was a graduate student in Castellano's laboratory during the research.
Some of the mice were genetically modified to lack TIMP2 throughout their bodies. In others, the researchers removed the protein specifically from either microglia or neurons. Comparing these models allowed the team to examine how TIMP2 influences immune cell behavior in both healthy and aging brains.
The scientists used several advanced techniques to study the changes. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing allowed them to examine patterns of gene activity in individual cell nuclei. They also used detailed imaging, functional tests, and a technique called in vivo microdialysis, which collects and measures substances from the fluid surrounding cells in living brain tissue.
The results revealed striking changes when TIMP2 was absent.
Microglia developed several features typically associated with aging and brain injury. Their cellular activation markers changed, their ability to remove debris declined, and they showed molecular signatures linked to cellular senescence, a biological state associated with aging and cellular stress.
The effects extended beyond the immune cells themselves. Using in vivo microdialysis, the researchers also detected higher levels of proteins associated with inflammation and stress in the extracellular environment surrounding brain cells.
Together, these findings indicated that TIMP2 helps prevent microglia from shifting toward potentially damaging states.
Restoring a Youth-Associated Protein Improves Aging Brain Cells
The researchers next explored whether supplying TIMP2 could counteract some of the changes observed with age.
They administered TIMP2 through injections to older mice, allowing the protein to circulate throughout the body. The treatment produced encouraging results.
Microglia became more effective at clearing cellular debris and showed a reduction in molecular markers associated with inflammatory states. In other words, restoring the youth-associated protein helped the aging immune cells recover some of the functions that normally deteriorate over time.
These improvements suggest that TIMP2 influences how microglia respond to conditions within the brain. By supporting their protective activities and limiting potentially harmful responses, the protein may help maintain a healthier environment for neurons.
The results also point to a possible biological connection between factors circulating in the body that are associated with youth and the activity of the brain's innate immune system. This system provides a first line of defense against injury and other threats.
A Potential New Direction for Brain Aging and Alzheimer's Research
The discovery adds to growing scientific interest in whether biological factors associated with youth can influence the aging process.
Because microglia help maintain brain health and can contribute to harmful inflammation when their behavior changes, finding ways to preserve their normal function could have important implications for understanding age-related neurological disorders.
"While additional studies are needed, this work provides new insight into how youth-associated factors influence pathways involved in brain aging and age-related neurological disorders that may ultimately inform therapeutic strategies," Dr. Castellano added.
However, the researchers caution that these findings come from experiments in mice. It remains unknown whether TIMP2 produces similar effects in humans or whether manipulating the protein could eventually become an effective treatment.
Additional studies will be necessary to determine whether TIMP2 itself, or the biological pathways it controls, can be targeted to reduce harmful changes associated with brain aging.
For now, the findings provide a promising new explanation for how a protein linked to youth helps maintain the brain's immune defenses, and how restoring it may recover some functions that weaken with age.
This work was supported by the National Institute on Aging (R01AG061382 (JMC), RF1AG072300 (JMC), 1F31AG079604-01A1 (BMH), T32AG049688 (BMH, SMP), R01AG061382-02S1 (JMC, SMP), and Cure Alzheimer's Fund (JMC).
Story Source:
Materials provided by The Mount Sinai Hospital / Mount Sinai School of Medicine. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Brittany M. Hemmer, Sarah M. Philippi, Ana Catarina Ferreira, Samuele F. Petridis, Annie Phan, Joseph M. Castellano. Youth-associated protein TIMP2 regulates microglial state and function in healthy and aged mice. Nature Communications, 2026; 17 (1) DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-74906-z

articles.title: Mọi người đều đã bị khái niệm "ngủ 8 tiếng lừa" rồi! Đâu là số giờ ngủ tốt nhất?
articles.text:
Theo huấn luyện viên giấc ngủ, việc theo đuổi giấc ngủ 8 tiếng là không cần thiết và cũng không nhất định sẽ tốt. Vậy, ngủ bao nhiêu là đủ? Đây là câu trả đúng nhất!
"Ăn ngon ngủ ngon là tiên", giấc ngủ là điều kiện tiên quyết để giữ gìn sức khỏe tốt, khoảng 1/3 cuộc đời của chúng ta là dành cho giấc ngủ, mà giấc ngủ cũng là một hoạt động sinh lý cần thiết hằng ngày. Nếu chúng ta ngủ đủ giấc và đều đặn thì cơ thể chúng ta mới có thể ở trạng thái khỏe mạnh.
Khi chúng ta già đi, thể trạng và thể lực của chúng ta sẽ không còn tốt như trước đây, cơ thể chúng ta sẽ bắt đầu xuất hiện các dấu hiệu lão hóa. Chất lượng giấc ngủ và sức khỏe của chúng ta có thể nói là có mối quan hệ rất mật thiết. Ngủ ngon, ngủ đủ giấc và đều đặn sẽ giúp tăng cường sức khỏe tốt hơn, ngược lại, những người ngủ không đủ giấc, thức đêm thường sẽ dễ khiến thể chất suy yếu.
Liệu bạn đã nghe nói về "khái niệm ngủ 8 tiếng" chưa? Trước giờ chúng ta đều được khuyên là nên ngủ đủ 8 tiếng mỗi ngày để có thể duy trì sức khỏe thể chất tốt, nhưng một số người đã đặt câu hỏi về điều này, họ cho rằng ngủ 8 tiếng mỗi ngày là một chuyện bịp.
Khoảng 1/3 cuộc đời của chúng ta là dành cho giấc ngủ. (Ảnh minh hoạ).
Huấn luyện viên giấc ngủ Nick Littlehales, người đã phụ trách theo dõi giấc ngủ cho Manchester United, đã đưa ra lời khuyên và hướng dẫn giấc ngủ khoa học cho các vận động viên của Manchester United để đảm bảo rằng các vận động viên có thể tự phục hồi trong khi ngủ, và có thể tối đa hóa thể chất cá nhân.
Vào thời điểm đó, Manchester United đã chinh phục được chức vô địch giải bóng đá ngoại hạng Anh 3 lần liên tiếp. Trong cuốn sách "cuộc cách mạng về giấc ngủ" của mình, Nick Littlehalles đã chỉ ra rằng việc theo đuổi giấc ngủ 8 tiếng là không cần thiết và cũng không nhất định sẽ tốt. Nguyên nhân chính là như sau:
1. Thể chất của mỗi người là khác nhau, do đó cũng cần thời gian ngủ khác nhau. Ngủ quá nhiều hoặc quá ít cũng sẽ gây hại cho sức khỏe. Cho nên, nếu cứ áp dụng kiến thức ngủ 8 tiếng cho tất cả 7 tỷ người trên thế giới thì rất có hại.
2. Ngủ đủ 8 tiếng mỗi đêm là không thực tế, đối với đại đa số học sinh, việc sắp xếp giấc ngủ 8 tiếng mỗi ngày là rất khó để thực hiện, thậm chí còn có thể gây thêm các trạng thái căng thẳng lo âu cho cơ thể.
3. Chất lượng giấc ngủ cần được đo bằng số chu kỳ giấc ngủ, nếu chỉ khăng khăng ngủ đủ 8 tiếng là vô nghĩa. Chu kỳ giấc ngủ kéo dài khoảng 90 phút, sau 90 phút, cơ thể sẽ trải qua giấc ngủ không chuyển động mắt, ngủ chuyển động mắt và ngủ chuyển động mắt nhanh. Nó giống như việc đi xuống cầu thang, khi con người đi xuống các tầng càng lúc càng sâu tức là cơ thể chúng ta cũng đang tiến vào tầng sâu hơn và sâu hơn nữa của giấc ngủ.
Do đó, bạn có thể thử kế hoạch ngủ R90 của các vận động viên hàng đầu được đề cập đến trong cuốn "cuộc cách mạng giấc ngủ". Kế hoạch ngủ linh hoạt của R90 đã được rất nhiều người ủng hộ thay vì khía niệm ngủ 8 giờ cứng nhắc.
Đối với người cao tuổi, rối loạn giấc ngủ luôn là vấn đề lớn nhất ảnh hưởng đến sức khỏe của họ. (Ảnh minh hoạ)
Đối với đại đa số người trung niên và người cao tuổi, rối loạn giấc ngủ luôn là vấn đề lớn nhất ảnh hưởng đến sức khỏe của họ, khi tuổi tác ngày càng cao, hệ thống thần kinh trung ương của não bộ dần suy yếu, chất lượng giấc ngủ cũng sẽ bị ảnh hưởng và suy giảm đi rất nhiều. Theo lời khuyên của bác sĩ, người trung niên và người cao tuổi nên ngủ đúng giờ trước 10h tối, trước khi đi ngủ có thể uống một ly sữa ấm, tốt nhất là 200ml.
Ngủ 6-7 tiếng mỗi ngày là đủ, đối với những người ngủ ít thì chỉ cần ngủ 5 tiếng rưỡi mỗi ngày. Theo nghiên cứu liên quan, người ta thấy rằng những người sau 60 tuổi không nên ép bản thân phải ngủ đủ 8 tiếng mỗi ngày, ngủ quá nhiều sẽ dễ làm tăng nguy cơ mắc bệnh Alzheimer. Ngược lại, mọi người cũng cần lưu ý, nếu thời gian ngủ không đủ, thậm chí còn dưới 5 tiếng, thì cũng sẽ có khả năng đẩy nhanh quá trình lão hóa của cơ thể và dễ tăng nguy cơ tử vong sớm.
Tổ chức Sleep Foundation của Hoa Kỳ đã phân tích thời gian ngủ theo từng nhóm tuổi khác nhau như sau:

articles.title: Lightest-ever neutron star system proves Einstein right about relativity yet again
articles.text:
Lightest-ever neutron star system proves Einstein right about relativity yet again
Einstein's theory of relativity just got put to the test by the lightest binary neutron star system ever discovered.
Astronomers have discovered the lightest known pair of neutron stars — two ultradense stellar remnants that circle each other every 2 hours, 22 minutes, veering toward an inevitable collision about 82 million years from now. By timing radio pulses from one of the stars, the researchers detected three subtle effects predicted by Albert Einstein's general theory of relativity and found that the theory describes the pair's motion to within about 1% — proving the visionary physicist right yet again.
The researchers published their findings Sept. 15 in the journal Physical Review Letters.
Neutron stars are the collapsed cores of massive stars that exploded as supernovas. Each packs more mass than the sun into a ball roughly 12 miles (20 kilometers) in diameter. Some, called pulsars, spin rapidly and sweep beams of radio waves across the sky like cosmic lighthouses. Their rotation is so steady that their pulses work as extraordinarily precise clocks.
Very few pulsars orbit another neutron star. "There are only 30 such double neutron star systems, and the relativistic effects are very strong if they are in compact orbits," study co-author JinLin Han, an astronomer at the National Astronomical Observatories of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, told Live Science via email.
The first such pair, discovered in 1974 and known as the Hulse-Taylor binary, provided the first evidence for gravitational waves — ripples in space-time predicted by Einstein. Such waves carry energy away from an orbiting pair, so its orbit should gradually shrink, and the Hulse-Taylor orbit shrank at just the rate Einstein's theory predicted.
Later, the "double pulsar," which completes an orbit every 2.45 hours, matched the predicted rate to within about 0.01%. Eventually, this shrinking forces such pairs to merge, unleashing gravitational waves like those the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo interferometer picked up in 2017.
A newly discovered pair
The new system, designated PSR J1856-0039, lies roughly 4,200 to 6,500 light-years from Earth. In 2020, it turned up in a survey of the Milky Way's disk by China's Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical Radio Telescope (FAST), the world's largest single-dish radio telescope.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.
"We have discovered about 900 pulsars," Han said of his team's work. "After a few follow-up observations, this one is very extraordinary."
The pulsar spins about 43 times per second, and the two stars are separated by roughly twice the distance between Earth and the moon. But the "most attractive feature" is the short orbital period of about 2.36 hours, Han said. "This is the second-shortest one, and it must show stronger relativistic effects than the famous double pulsar and the Hulse-Taylor system."
The team observed the pair with FAST 17 times between 2020 and 2025, sometimes long enough to cover a whole orbit. The researchers measured the arrival times of the system's pulses and then fit that data to orbital models that accounted for relativistic effects, like subtle changes to the pulse arrival times at different parts of the stars' orbits.
"With so many measurements by FAST, which would be hard to match in accuracy with other telescopes, we got not only the basic parameters of the pulsar and its orbit but also three relativistic effects," Han said.
First, the orbit is shrinking as the stars radiate gravitational waves, drawing them about 9 feet (2.7 meters) closer each year. Second, the oval orbit turns slowly, by 17.6 degrees per year — some 150,000 times faster than the relativistic drift of Mercury's orbit. Third, because both gravity and speed slow time, the pulsar's clock runs at a varying pace along the oval orbit, shifting its pulses by up to about half a millisecond.
"From these measurements, we determined the pulsar mass and the companion mass," Han explained. "The total mass is the lowest among all known double neutron star systems." The pulsar weighs about 1.3 times as much as the sun, and its companion is just 1.19 solar masses — one of the lowest-mass neutron stars known. Simulations suggest that supernovas can't forge neutron stars much lighter than that.
The stars will merge in about 82 million years. That merger will probably leave behind a heavier neutron star of about 2.26 solar masses, though the remnant could instead collapse into a black hole, the researchers estimate.
Another win for Einstein
Any two of the three effects are enough to calculate both stars' masses. The third then serves as an independent check, because if general relativity is correct, all three must point to the same masses — and they do.
Related stories
"We found that general relativity is needed to explain the data, and the consistency is about 1%," Han said. The double pulsar test is more precise, but it drew on 16 years of data, compared with about five for the new pair. "Unfortunately, we could not beat this description of gravity," Han added, referring to physicists' hope of finding cracks in Einstein's theory that might reveal new physics.
Next, the team hopes to detect "frame dragging," an effect in which a spinning mass twists space-time around it, making nearby orbits wobble. "In the future, we will monitor this pulsar, probably over decades, to detect the frame dragging induced by the neutron star's spin," Han said.
Measuring the effect would reveal the pulsar's moment of inertia, which depends on how its mass is spread out inside. That would provide "a novel constraint" on how matter behaves at the crushing densities in neutron star cores, Han said — one of the biggest open questions in physics.

Relativistic effects of PSR J1856–0039 double neutron star system in a 2.36-Hour compact orbit. Physical Review Letters, 137(12), 121401. https://doi.org/10.1103/hmjp-htd1

Andrey got his B.Sc. and M.Sc. degrees in elementary particle physics from Novosibirsk State University in Russia, and a Ph.D. in string theory from the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel. He works as a science writer, specializing in physics, space, and technology. His articles have been published in AdvancedScienceNews, PhysicsWorld, Science, and other outlets.

articles.title: NASA’s SpaceX launch lights up the sky with a giant glowing jellyfish
articles.text:
NASA’s SpaceX launch lights up the sky with a giant glowing jellyfish
- Date:
- October 17, 2026
- Source:
- NASA
- Summary:
- A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket created a dazzling, jellyfish-shaped glow across the eastern United States as sunlight illuminated its exhaust during an early morning launch. The mission delivered equipment and scientific experiments to the International Space Station, including research that could advance treatments for blindness, Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and other diseases.
- Share:
A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket transformed the early morning sky into a spectacular display of light on October 13, 2026. As the rocket climbed above Earth carrying a Dragon spacecraft, sunlight illuminated its expanding exhaust plumes, creating an enormous glowing shape that resembled a jellyfish.
This striking phenomenon, known as a "jellyfish," occurs when a rocket launches near sunrise or sunset. Sunlight reaches the exhaust high in the atmosphere, making the spreading plume shine brightly against the darker sky below.
See a wider view of the "jellyfish."
SpaceX Launch Creates a Spectacular Sky Display
The mission lifted off at 6:33 a.m. EDT from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. The illuminated exhaust plumes were visible across the eastern United States, giving observers a remarkable view of the rocket's journey into space.
The launch marked SpaceX's 35th commercial resupply mission for NASA, delivering scientific experiments, essential supplies, and equipment to the International Space Station.
New Space Station Upgrades and Medical Experiments
Among the cargo aboard Dragon is the final set of International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Arrays, known as IROSAs. These additional solar panels are scheduled for installation later this fall and will help provide electricity for the orbiting laboratory.
The spacecraft is also transporting equipment for several scientific investigations that could lead to important advances in medicine and materials science.
One experiment will explore manufacturing artificial retinas in microgravity, where the near absence of gravity creates conditions that cannot easily be reproduced on Earth. The research could help develop technologies to restore vision in people with certain forms of vision loss.
Another investigation will use 3D heart tissue models to support the development of more efficient drug testing methods during future space missions.
Additional experiments will examine how a new type of glass forms in microgravity and investigate brain organoids, miniature models of brain tissue grown from cells. These models could help researchers identify new targets for treating neurological conditions, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and multiple sclerosis.
