articles.title: BlackRock's Rick Rieder sees 'historic' opportunity in high-quality bonds
articles.text:
Investors may be wary of the volatility hitting parts of the bond market right now, but they have an "historic" opportunity to grab attractive yields in high-quality credit, Rick Rieder, BlackRock's chief investment officer for global fixed income, told CNBC in an exclusive interview.
Hypothetically, it's now possible for investors to build a diversified portfolio that yields more than 7% with less than three years of duration and an average credit quality of A-, he said. Duration is a measurement of a bond's price sensitivity to fluctuations in rates, and issues with shorter maturities tend to have lower duration.
"Not only is it historic in that these yields are where they are, but the only time these yields are ever here is when there's some problem, like an economic problem or default problem," Rieder said in an interview about his fourth-quarter outlook, released Wednesday.
That isn't the case now, where the economy remains strong, he said. "So you don't really have to worry about defaults of any significance."
While Rieder didn't specifically identify the credits in the aforementioned portfolio, the iShares Aaa - A Rated Corporate Bond ETF (QLTA) has a 30-day SEC yield of 5.68% and an effective duration of 6.48 years — higher than Rieder's low duration focus.
The iShares Flexible Income Active ETF (BINC), which is managed by Rieder, has a 5.66% 30-day SEC yield and three-year effective duration, but its portfolio extends beyond investment-grade credit.
Best opportunities include hyperscalers
Rieder sees the best opportunity right now in investment-grade corporate bonds — which he pointed out he hasn't said "in a really long time." Investment grade bonds are rated AAA through BBB- by S&P and Fitch, while Moody's rates them Aaa through Baa3.
That includes hyperscaler bonds, which have flooded the market with issuance this year as they ramp up their AI infrastructure. Alphabet, Amazon, Meta Platforms and Oracle have issued a total of about $228.4 billion in bonds year to date, as of Oct. 20, according to LSEG.
"They're very low leverage. They have tremendous amounts of cash flow coming in," Rieder said of the hyperscalers in general. "You're now getting to buy these entities which are higher quality, paying you a very attractive yield to get it."
Rieder's iShares Flexible Income Active ETF has upped its allocation to investment-grade corporates to 14.3% of its portfolio. In July, that stood at 8.5%.
That said, investors need to be patient and sit tight since rates could still move higher from here, he advised.
"Your starting point is by far your best barometer of what your return is going to be," he noted. "So if you get seven and a quarter, maybe you get eight, maybe you get six, but ... if your holding period is a year or longer, you're going to get that yield."
Caution should also be exercised outside of investment-grade credit, which requires more selectivity and deep research, he warned. That includes AI names.
"There's parts of the data center supply that's not hyperscaler guaranteed or hyperscaler backed," he said. "That we've been more cautious around, and we'll continue to be."
The bond market, particularly high-yield credit, has been rocked as investor concern grows over the massive amount of debt some companies are taking out to fund their artificial intelligence build-out.
Junk-rated CoreWeave has become the poster child, seeing its stock drop, bond yields jump and credit-default spreads widen. Oracle, which is sitting in the lower end of investment grade and is seen as a bellwether on the broader AI market, has also taken some hits.
Fed watch
Rieder is also keeping an eye on the Federal Reserve, which is expected to raise its federal funds rate again in December to combat inflation. The market is currently pricing in a nearly 90% probability that the central bank will hike at that time, according to the CME Group FedWatch tool.
The money manager expects that to happen, although he does not agree with it. Higher rates are hurting parts of the economy, like housing, while not having much of an impact on other areas — such as tech companies' capital expenditures, which have become a big driver of growth, he said.
"They're not borrowing off the overnight funds rate," Rieder noted. "There's a lot of floating rate finance in housing, credit card, auto loan finance, and you're seeing those areas already under pressure."
Instead, the market is and will continue to price the AI supply coming into the market, he added.
Calculating risks ahead
Rieder sees a number of possible risks ahead, including rising levels of government debt across the globe. In the United States, the budget deficit has grown to $2 trillion for fiscal 2026.
"The more the central banks raise the rates, the cost of debt to these to already indebted governments is something we've got to be careful about over time," he said.
Bond supply coming from AI companies should also be watched.
"With the amount of supply that's coming — data center, hyperscaler — there's some crowding-out effect that's taking place," he said. "With government rates moving higher, that is something that we just got to keep an eye on."
In the meantime, Rieder would just continue to reap the rewards of high investment-grade yields "and smile a lot," he said.

articles.title: SpaceX gives the AI trade a shot in the arm. What it means for our stocks
articles.text: Listening to Elon Musk on SpaceX's earnings call sounded like the basis of a best-selling science fiction novel. But what this rocket, artificial intelligence, and global connectivity company is doing in the real world is big business. And there are far-reaching implications for a bunch of the biggest stocks in our portfolio. SpaceX shares are soaring 7% on Wednesday after the company reported strong third-quarter results with a robust outlook through year-end and into 2027. Musk's sprawling brainchild, which he wants to merge with his EV and solar company Tesla, gives SpaceX access and insight into so many of the various industries currently powering the stock market — pretty much every level of the five-layer AI cake that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang talks about, from power to semiconductors, to data center infrastructure, to AI models and applications. Layer in Musk's visionary nature and ability to get investors excited, and you're left with an earnings conference call that should be considered required reading for any market participant. After all, AI now touches so much of the market and economy more broadly that whether you're a top-down macro investor or bottom-up fundamental investor, you need to have some view on where AI spending goes from here. Now, let's examine what Musk said as a read-through to the Club names that sit across the various layers of the AI cake. Data center suppliers Unlike the earlier days of the AI boom, semiconductor availability is no longer the major issue constraining compute supply, Musk said. "I think people are starting to realize the constraint on deployment of super intelligence is more in power and cooling and infrastructure than it is in chips," he said, using President Donald Trump's preferred term for artificial intelligence. In September, Trump signed an executive order instructing all executive branch departments and agencies to use "SI" instead of AI. Musk has embraced the president's rebrand internally at SpaceX, and he uses the term in multiple quotes throughout this story. Musk's constraint commentary is very much in line with a Business Insider report from earlier this week, which said Amazon is racing to buy AI hardware to ensure it has enough, even as it lacks the power infrastructure required to actually get that compute online. Musk said SpaceX has redeployed some of its engineers — the same ones behind the company's wildly successful rocket-ship innovations — to solve the power and cooling bottlenecks. "It's a team that has been able to achieve results that are an order of magnitude greater than the rest of all competitors in space combined and applied that same team to the deployment of terrestrial compute. So, this is a bit like the New York Yankees playing in Little League. It's not fair." As a result, he claimed SpaceX is "able to deploy power cooling infrastructure at a rate that is vastly faster than anyone else and may, at some point, be faster than everyone else combined." SpaceX plans to bring on between 2.5 and 3 gigawatts of compute power by the end of the year, according to Musk. Looking to next year, Musk said he is "fairly confident" in being able to bring 10 GW of additional compute in 2027, but suggested much more could be possible. A gigawatt of power can provide electricity to more than 750,000 homes for a year. "There's a non-zero possibility ... of SpaceX having over 20 gigawatts of super intelligence compute online next year. A small possibility. It used to be zero. It's not zero anymore," he said. Why do we care? Because if he is going to achieve his goals, he is going to need a lot more of the components needed to do it. And while SpaceX appears able to make some of what it needs in-house — like blades and vanes for gas-powered turbines — the ambitious targets also point to upside demand for companies like Club names GE Vernova and Eaton . GE Vernova is a leading maker of heavy-duty gas turbines, and Eaton provides all sorts of electrical and cooling equipment used across the grid and inside data centers. Agentic demand SpaceX's earnings also served as an appetizer of sorts for Meta Platforms' report on Wednesday night. Within its AI business, SpaceX has social media site X, recently acquired coding assistant Cursor, and the Grok chatbot. In August, the company officially launched an agentic AI offering known as Grok Bot, which is similar to Meta's Muse. These agentic systems are capable of completing multi-step tasks with little to no human intervention, and they represent a sizable advancement over the generative AI chatbots of a few years ago. "We're seeing the fastest growth of a product that I've ever seen in my life for Grok Bot," Musk said. I've never seen anything grow this fast. We're also seeing that the usage of Grok Bot grows over time per user. It does not decline. So, as we make Grok Bot more useful, we're seeing users use it more per week, not use it less." Grok Bot "already had paid weekly users of 800,000 earlier this month, more than doubling over the last month," President and COO Gwynne Shotwell said on the call. Musk also said, "I think Grok Bot may end up being what uses most of our Super Intelligence compute." We'll be comparing that commentary against what Meta has to say about Muse on Wednesday night. The Muse launch in September was met with much praise as the app quickly surged to the top of Apple's App Store downloads list. However, commentary on retention will be critical for investors. Usage matters far more to the long-term AI story than initial downloads. The market is also wondering whether Meta will disclose any concrete figures on Muse usage and paid sign-ups. We would love to get that information, so let's hope Meta follows SpaceX's lead in this regard. On a similar note, we're interested to hear what Muse means for Meta's compute needs and spending plans going forward. Chipmakers and cloud providers Musk's commentary on Grok Bot usage also points to sustained demand for the semiconductors that make AI possible. Just because they aren't the central constraint anymore doesn't mean they're not important. They certainly are. This includes both AI accelerators like Nvidia's graphics processing units (GPUs) and Alphabet's tensor processing units (TPUs), along with workhorse central processing units (CPUs) and memory chips. Agentic AI requires way more CPUs and memory than predecessor systems. That bodes well for the year ahead as far as our semiconductor names are concerned. Here we're talking about Nvidia on the GPU front, Intel on the CPU front, Micron for its high-bandwidth memory, and Broadcom for its custom silicon work, including on Google's TPUs. Nvidia and Broadcom also stand to benefit on the networking front, as we are long past the days when compute was about a single chip or server. One of the big concerns in recent weeks has been whether all this spending on AI infrastructure will deliver adequate returns to justify more spending. On this debate, SpaceX's comments indicate that pricing power for those selling compute is only improving. "What we're seeing in the market is extraordinary," CFO Bret Johnsen said. "At current pricing, new compute deployments are generating a payback of less than a year. Pricing is currently tracking slightly above the high end of the $30 to $50 per watt range we were discussing just last quarter, which further supports the attractiveness of these terrestrial SI compute investments." That bodes well for the hardware players because it means demand is as strong, if not stronger, than it was just three months ago. For the hyperscaler players with cloud businesses like Microsoft , Alphabet, and Amazon , it means the return on capex could come even quicker than Wall Street was expecting. We will certainly be looking out for similar commentary as those reports come in next week. Bottom line While we're not aggressively bullish right now as the AI trade still works through other headwinds (namely those of the political variety), SpaceX's earnings report is incredibly supportive of the theme going forward. We acknowledge Musk always puts out very ambitious targets and timelines, like the ability to get 20GW of compute online next year. However, that doesn't negate the fact that what SpaceX is seeing on the ground, in the here and now, is accelerating demand for AI solutions. That, in turn, is driving strong pricing power for those able to supply the compute, whether that's the semiconductor companies or the power and cooling solutions providers needed to get and keep chips running. Combine this with the view we shared earlier this week — that we see no change in the long usable life of these chips — and Tuesday night's SpaceX call served as another win for the bulls because it provided further confirmation that the fundamentals of the AI investment cycle remain very much intact. (Jim Cramer's Charitable Trust is long NVDA, MU, ETN, GEV, META. See here for a full list of the stocks.) articles.title: Apple's iPhone Duo in short supply — plus, the 2 stocks fueling an AI rebound
articles.text: Every weekday, the CNBC Investing Club with Jim Cramer releases the Homestretch — an actionable afternoon update, just in time for the last hour of trading on Wall Street. Stocks are moving solidly higher , putting the S & P 500 and Nasdaq on track for their third consecutive winning session. Wednesday's action marked a strong rebound in the AI infrastructure trade, with technology stocks and industrials tied to the data center buildout leading the market higher. Part of the move can be traced back to strong earnings and bullish commentary from SpaceX , which is becoming a major AI hyperscaler in addition to its rocket launch and satellite operations. CEO Elon Musk indicated on the SpaceX earnings call that power, cooling, and electrical equipment are the limiting factors in getting more gigawatts of compute online, which had investors feeling better about the outlooks for stocks like GE Vernova , Eaton , and Vertiv . In addition, Super Micro Computer preannounced much stronger-than-expected quarterly revenue, which helped the tech hardware sector rebound. Cybersecurity stocks are gaining amid growing concerns that AI tools are making it easier and faster to discover software vulnerabilities. As money rotated back into AI stocks, it moved out of defensive sectors like healthcare and consumer staples. Johnson & Johnson , Kimberly Clark , and Eli Lilly gave back some of their recent gains. Energy prices and interest rates were also mostly out of the picture, with WTI crude oil prices falling about $1 per barrel and the yield on the 10-year Treasury dipping slightly. Apple said it will have limited quantities of its new foldable iPhone Duo available for walk-in customers when it hits stores Friday, Reuters reported . The company is also capping purchases at two per customer. The company is also capping purchases at two devices per customer. With wait times to receive the Duo now exceeding three months, we view this as a function of both strong demand and supply constraints. This latest iPhone appears to have been better received than expected, despite its $1,999 price tag. However, limited inventory may be a bottleneck, forcing some customers to wait months to get their hands on it. We'll know more about the Duo when Apple reports earnings on Nov. 2, but this is still an own-it, don't-trade-it story for us. We predict the Duo will be another growth engine for Apple . Meta Platforms reports after the close , and we'll be listening for what the company says about engagement with its new personal AI agent, Muse, capital expenditure trends, and the possibility of an equity raise to fund its AI infrastructure buildout. Lam Research is another notable company reporting, and what this semiconductor capital equipment maker has to say about demand for advanced memory and logic chips could sway sentiment in Club stocks such as Micron , Intel , and Qnity Electronics . articles.title: The AI trade may be at a turning point. Where it may go, and how to play it
articles.text: (See the video above for Todd's complete chart breakdown.) We're at a genuinely interesting juncture in the market. Since early summer, we've tracked a steady rotation out of technology and into value, a theme I've covered often in this weekly column. This week we leaned into it and trimmed 13.5% from the artificial intelligence-related portion of our growth portfolio, added to energy and healthcare as discussed last week in this column, and placed a modest 5% hedge against the Nasdaq via the PSQ ETF . Then came Tuesday's blowout SpaceX earnings, and growth roared back. So the question we have to answer as active portfolio managers is: Was that a turning point, or a bounce into resistance? In the video, I walk through the two charts I'm using to answer it. The first is a ratio chart, which is one of the best tools for gauging relative strength. A price chart tells you whether something went up. A ratio chart tells you whether it went up more than the alternative you could have owned. Divide one asset by another, like semis by the S & P 500 , and the line rises only when the first is outperforming. Portfolios are built on percentage returns, not dollar moves, so the ratio cuts straight to the question that matters: Where should the next dollar go? This chart tracks the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) against both the S & P 500 (SPY) and the Nasdaq-100 (QQQ) over the past year. Both ratios peaked around June 1, and semis have lagged both benchmarks since, AI build-out notwithstanding. Now, both ratios are sitting right on support. A break below those highlighted zones would confirm the rotation out of semis is continuing, a risk-off signal that favors value-oriented sectors. The second chart is the more traditional daily view of the Nasdaq-100. Here, a double top has formed between the June and September highs, followed by a break of the uptrend line (dashed red) and the 21- and 50-day moving averages. The SpaceX rally is now pushing the Nasdaq-100 back up from below to retest that broken support, which may now act as resistance near 30,000. Given our positioning, I believe that resistance holds. If I'm wrong, we'll lift the hedge and redeploy the 13.5% we trimmed, likely at higher prices. That's the honest trade-off of active management at a tricky juncture like this, and we'll keep feeling our way through it. Todd Gordon is the founder of Inside Edge Capital, LLC. articles.title: Netflix has dipped its toe into theatrical. Is it ready to jump in?
articles.text:
Netflix is making itself clear: It's a streaming-first business.
During the company's third-quarter earnings call on Tuesday, co-CEO Ted Sarandos reiterated the streaming giant's long-held stance that its content, which it spent $20 billion on last year, is meant for its subscribers and, therefore, should be delivered to customers on its streaming platform as quickly as possible.
Yet, the company is set to have 30 theatrical releases in 2027, on par with what it brought to cinemas in 2026. And while not all of these features are expected to have wide releases or long runs in theaters, Netflix is testing the waters with projects like Greta Gerwig's "Narnia: The Magician's Nephew," which will have a wide release and a 49-day exclusive theatrical window when it hits cinemas in February.
The company seems poised to carve a new path forward as it grapples with viewership stagnation and a stock slump of roughly 30% since January.
How its theatrical ambitions fit into a streaming-first strategy remains a question mark.
"Theatrical releases are a net positive for reach and streaming demand," Alicia Reese, analyst at Wedbush, wrote in a note Wednesday. "Netflix's more amenable attitude toward exclusive theatrical windows will not only facilitate better relationships with talent, but also add a new revenue stream and build interest in its streaming service. This follows the pattern we have seen with the major studios' streaming platforms over the past several years: theatrical releases don't cannibalize the streaming window, as Netflix fears."
Ahead of its Tuesday earnings report, Netflix restructured its C-suite, bringing in former Disney executive Peter Rice to take over as the company's chief content officer, ousting 10-year veteran Bela Bajaria.
Netflix also dismissed Dan Lin, the company's head of film, according to a person familiar with the matter who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss internal changes. That came just days after it laid off roughly 1,000 employees including Lin's right hand Doug Belgrad as well as Sheroum Kim, the director of independent film, according to various media reports. It's unclear who Netflix will tap to take over Lin's position.
The company aims to restore quality to the brand and utilize Rice's expertise in talent relations to lure big names in an increasingly competitive market.
Still, Netflix executives seemed to downplay the change in leadership during the company's earnings call.
"Our business and our business flywheel are working," Sarandos told investors during the company's earnings call. "There is no need for a fundamental shift in the strategy. We do need better execution in the U.S. ... It's just not growing as fast as it could or as fast as we'd like."
Sarandos said the streamer had "some really solid doubles and triples this year," but suggested the company needs more "home runs."
In an emblematic moment during Tuesday's call, Sarandos highlighted a deal with Disney, struck in October, to bring the Ice Age films and others to the streaming service, and gave a nod to that company's CEO, Josh D'Amaro.
"We already are seeing some of those benefits from the Ice Age movies. All five of them hit our top 10. That's really exciting," the Netflix co-CEO said. "And by the way, yes, Netflix just plugged a Disney movie on our earnings call. You're welcome, Josh."
Netflix's content strategy
In a bid to capture consumer attention and broaden its subscriber funnel, Netflix has spent years diversifying its offerings to include video games, live sports and quick-turn documentaries on buzzy cultural moments.
But more recently, it's lacked some of the water-cooler-type hits like "Stranger Things," "Bridgerton" and "Squid Game" that previously boosted subscriptions and viewership numbers.
"We know there's some investor concern about our view hours growth," Netflix said in its shareholder letter Tuesday. "Engagement — which encompasses quantity, quality and variety of viewing — remains healthy."
And yet with Netflix stating plainly that it needs new avenues for growth — and against the backdrop of a foiled deal to buy the Warner Bros. film studio — investors and onlookers are once again looking at the theatrical business.
"I think there's a place for the theatrical for Netflix," Matthew Condon, equity research analyst at Citizens, told CNBC. "Especially, as the competition for time and attention just continues to increase."
"If they really want to build stickier fan bases around some of their [intellectual property], I think theatrical could be a good avenue for them to do that," Condon said. "That's one area that Netflix has historically not been all that strong in, is building like really, really strong IP. And I think building fan bases around theatrical releases and things of that nature can help with that and then also can help them get top tier talent."
Netflix is no stranger to luring in big Hollywood directors. It's worked with the likes of Rian Johnson, Martin Scorsese, Alfonso Cuarón, Bong Joon Ho, Spike Lee and Guillermo del Toro. However, none of these directors' Netflix films received a wide theatrical release or a long run in theaters.
Sarandos admitted earlier this month that the company has lost talent because it would not guarantee wide theatrical releases.
Most notably, the creators and lead producer behind its hit "Stranger Things" have all jumped ship in the last year. Matt and Ross Duffer signed a four-year exclusive deal with Skydance — the new home of the same Warner Bros. film studio that Netflix nearly bought — while Shawn Levy joined the ranks of Disney to direct "Star Wars: Starfighter."
Going to the movies
Sarandos said Tuesday the company's strategy is about "specialty theatrical releasing," in which each film gets its own bespoke release. In some cases, Netflix plays the film in theaters for the minimum requirement to be eligible for awards. Others appear for weekend stints as one-off events, like in the case of its "KPop Demon Hunters" smash that ran in theaters for just two days.
Gerwig's "Narnia" adaptation is among those chosen few to get longer theatrical runs and a wider reach, along with an animated film called "Charlie vs. the Chocolate Factory."
"Both films have big global IP and big global fandom, so we're very excited about how they'll play out next year," Sarandos said.
In another sign of its evolution into theaters, Netflix has said it will report box office results for films that have longer theatrical windows. Those readouts are standard for major studios, regardless of release or windowing, but the move marks a new level of disclosure for the streamer.
Incoming content head Rice could be the missing piece for Netflix in a new theatrical model.
The executive has a wealth of experience in television and film. Since 2023 he has produced films like "Saturday Night" and "28 Years Later." He's currently developing a movie adaptation of the video game "Elden Ring."
But right now, Netflix doesn't have the infrastructure for a full theatrical commitment.
"Going into theatrical isn't quite as easy as I think sometimes folks make it sound," Steven Cahall, stock analyst at Wells Fargo, told CNBC. "You have to negotiate with movie theaters, and find spots for your films."
Cahall noted that sending the occasional film to theaters, especially with a limited release, "maybe isn't so hard, but there is a muscle of theatrical distribution ... You need a team of people, and you need a pipeline of content that's intended for theatrical release, and you need a marketing department around it."
That's where buying Warner Bros. Discovery's studio assets would have come in. In the absence of that acquisition, it's not clear how, or how quickly, Netflix can bulk up its own operations.
Plus, it's previously balked at the marketing costs that come with bringing films to the cinema, which can total hundreds of millions of dollars per film. Despite a hefty content budget, Netflix has long prioritized quantity and seemingly endless choice for its subscribers over individual big-budget projects.
A shift to a multi-pronged strategy that feeds both streaming and cinemas would require Netflix to more closely mimic the companies it disrupted in the first place.
"So that becomes more of an existential question for Netflix: Is it time to become a media conglomerate rather than being a pure play streaming company?" Wells Fargo's Cahall said. "'Do we want to become a media conglomerate?'"

articles.title: Anthropic appoints physicist Christopher Stubbs to its Long-Term Benefit Trust
articles.text:
Anthropic on Wednesday announced it has appointed the experimental physicist Christopher Stubbs to its Long-Term Benefit Trust, which helps elect the company's board members and advise its leadership.
Stubbs is a professor of physics and astronomy at Harvard University, where he previously served as the dean of science. His research explores subjects like gravitational physics, dark matter, dark energy and observational cosmology, according to Harvard's website. Stubbs is the first physicist to join Anthropic's Trust.
"I'm using AI tools in my research every day, and the doors they're opening for science are incredible," Stubbs wrote in a post on LinkedIn on Wednesday. "As a teacher, I'm also confronting some of the challenging questions they raise. As a grandfather, I want the generation growing up with AI to be better off for it."
Stubbs' appointment comes as Anthropic is gearing up for what is widely expected to be a massive IPO. The company confidentially filed its prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June, and it has been engaging in meetings with prospective investors in recent weeks. Anthropic announced plans to commit 5% of its shares to a new public benefit fund on Sunday, with the potential for more to be added at its board's discretion.
Anthropic's Long-Term Benefit Trust is financially independent from the company's management and investors, and has the ability to appoint "a majority" of Anthropic's board, according to a blog post. The company said trustees also advise board members and other leadership, especially around the "societal impacts of AI."
In addition to Stubbs, Anthropic's Trust includes Ben Bernanke, the former chair of the Federal Reserve, Neil Buddy Shah, CEO of the Clinton Health Access Initiative, and Richard Fontaine, a national security expert.
"I'm so grateful for the chance to help carry out this important work," Stubbs said.

articles.title: Capital One delivered a strong quarter. Why we're not declaring victory just yet
articles.text: Capital One is finally getting credit for a solid quarter, but the debate surrounding the credit card giant's stock is far from settled. Shares of Capital One jumped roughly 4% on Wednesday after the company delivered better-than-expected third-quarter results , supported by resilient consumer credit, progress integrating Discover, and stronger net interest income (NII) — the difference between what a bank makes on loans, like credit card interest in the case of Capital One, and what pays out on deposits. The rally was welcome news for a stock that has struggled — down 13.5% year to date. The quarterly results and post-earnings conference call commentary Tuesday evening offered a clearer picture of Capital One's earnings potential. But they didn't resolve one of our biggest concerns: elevated spending. While a bit lighter than expected, total company marketing expense did rise 14% year-over-year to $1.6 billion. Management expects marketing costs to increase sequentially from the third quarter to the fourth quarter at a similar growth rate of 35.7% during the same quarter-over-quarter period last year — primarily driven by seasonality. On the call, CEO Richard Fairbank said Capital One plans to "lean harder" into marketing in 2027 as it pursues growth in premium credit cards, national banking, and the Discover franchise. The company did not disclose a marketing expense estimate for next year. "Our biggest competitors continue to invest heavily in marketing, and we need to be at the top of our game," the CEO added. It's a strategy we understand and recently wrote about : Capital One is investing to attract more affluent, high-spending customers. Those investments could create more profitable customer relationships over time, but they come at a near-term cost. Bank of America analysts said in a note Wednesday to clients that "the spend is right for the franchise, but with no efficiency guidance, COF [Capital One] must show it does not erode the earnings power it has just revealed." Deutsche Bank echoed those concerns, lowering its 2027 earnings estimate to $22.25 per share from $22.50 due to anticipated marketing spending. That uncertainty was a major reason we trimmed our Capital One position Tuesday ahead of earnings and downgraded the stock to our hold-equivalent 2 rating . The sale wasn't a prediction about the quarter but rather a reflection of our frustration with how much upfront spending has been required to unlock growth from the Discover and Brex acquisitions. "Expenses have been part of the issue that's been hanging over the stock for the past year," portfolio analyst Jeff Marks said during Wednesday's Morning Meeting . In light of the rally, he added that Tuesday's trim was a bit ill-timed. However, a profit is still a profit. The sale represented a roughly 13% gain on Capital One stock purchased in March 2025. COF YTD mountain Capital One YTD The good news is that the Discover integration is progressing faster than expected. Capital One has achieved roughly $1.8 billion in annualized synergies, with the benefits of moving debit transactions onto its own payment network and eliminating overlapping costs becoming increasingly apparent. The target at the time the $35 billion Discover deal was announced in February 2024 was a combined $2.7 billion of synergies in 2027. "We're achieving the expected synergies ahead of schedule," Fairbank said. "We have talked for a while now about the earnings power on the other side of integration. You can squint your eyes and see it now in the first three quarters of 2026." Discover card originations also increased year over year for the first time since the deal closed, while Capital One's swipe-fee revenue continued to climb. Owning the Discover payment network allows the company to collect more of the fees merchants pay when customers use their cards — like American Express , which issues cards and owns its payment network. There is one new complication. Capital One expects to lose some swipe-fee revenue if a proposed Visa and Mastercard settlement with merchants receives final approval. Visa and Mastercard do not issue credit cards. They provide the payment rails. Banks — like Amex, Capital One, Citigroup , and many others — are the ones issuing the cards. Capital One management said that headwind would roughly offset the remaining Discover synergies. Morgan Stanley said in a Wednesday note that the potential loss of roughly $700 million in swipe-fee revenue "overshadowed" an otherwise strong quarter. Adjusted earnings of $6.69 per share easily beat the $5.50 consensus estimate, while revenue of $16.34 billion also topped expectations. Credit performance was particularly encouraging given concerns that elevated oil prices and inflation could pressure consumers. However, a $225 million reserve release helped boost earnings, meaning investors shouldn't expect that level of profitability every quarter. "We appreciate the solid results, but would not annualize a seasonally favorable quarter ahead of higher marketing and interchange pressure," Baird Equity Research said in a note to clients Wednesday. Despite the spending concerns, Capital One remains attractively valued at less than 9 times consensus 2027 earnings estimates. The company also repurchased another $2.6 billion in shares during the quarter, providing additional support for shareholders. "The main thing here is really it's cheap," Jeff said Wednesday. "There's a nice plan in place. Investing in growth. We'll never truly fault a company for wanting to invest in growth." Bottom line For now, we're holding on to our remaining shares, encouraged by the progress on Discover and resilient credit performance but mindful that higher spending could continue to constrain earnings growth. Capital One is getting closer to realizing the benefits of its transformative acquisition. The challenge going forward is making sure the cost of pursuing its next phase of growth doesn't overshadow the hard-fought gains the company has already made. articles.title: GM aims to develop vehicles in as little as two years with AI, software push
articles.text:
NEW YORK — General Motors plans to lean into artificial intelligence and vehicle software for future growth and development amid increasing competition abroad from Chinese automakers and a tougher U.S. market.
The Detroit automaker on Wednesday shared new details about a proprietary AI agent it's releasing under its OnStar brand, plans for a fourth generation of more efficient all-electric vehicles and a target to cut its vehicle development time in half.
GM also reconfirmed that by 2028, it wants to have eyes-off highway driving, or "personal autonomy," that will let drivers take their attention off the road. The automaker said that technology would start with the Cadillac Escalade IQ EV before rolling out to other, more high-volume models.
"All of these developments are building us the car of the future," CEO Mary Barra said Wednesday during an event laying out the plans, called "GM Forward," in downtown Manhattan.
The initiatives, which Barra, Chief Product Officer Sterling Anderson and other executives discussed at the event, are designed to streamline the automaker's operations, while also improving the capabilities of its vehicles for customers.
"Over the last 12 months, we've evolved how we design, engineer and build our vehicles," said Anderson, who led the event and who has been tasked with overseeing GM's latest technology transformation.
GM said it is now targeting a vehicle development time of roughly two years from concept to production versus a traditional four- to five-year cycle. However, the company did not detail a timeline for reaching that goal.
The event comes as Chinese automakers are growing outside of the U.S. with rapid development times of new technologies and vehicles. Consulting firm AlixPartners said it believes China is currently bringing vehicles to market twice as fast as traditional automakers, with 40% to 50% less investment and a 30% cost advantage.
GM also continues to play catch-up to U.S. EV leader Tesla when it comes to delivering technology advancements through over-the-air updates and automated driving capabilities.
Anderson, a former Tesla executive, declined to speak specifically about how GM's technologies will compare to the EV maker, but said GM's systems will be able to visualize, or see, more things through the use of multiple types of sensors than a strictly camera-based system, which Tesla uses.
He also said the rapid development and new software architecture will help the company better compete against Chinese automakers abroad.
"There's inherent virtue to speed," Anderson told CNBC during an interview after the event. "Not just in being able to get a car out faster, it's being able to develop a system that's far more performant that you could have otherwise."
Next-generation vehicles
GM said Wednesday it has major plans for its next generation of EVs and traditional vehicles with internal combustion engines.
The company said those coming vehicles — regardless of type — will have 40 times the computing power and up to 50% faster cellular connectivity than prior systems.
That computing power is expected to help the automaker with over-the-air updates, onboard diagnostics and AI, as well as other technologies such as automated driving features.
The new brain of the vehicle will launch on the $130,000 Cadillac Escalade IQ EV in 2028 before rolling out to other models, including its next generation of EVs.
GM said the forthcoming EVs are expected to be 25% more aerodynamic and 15% lighter and feature electric motors and battery packs that are more compact.
GM President Mark Reuss said despite lackluster consumer adoption and the automaker pulling back billions of dollars in investments in EVs, it remains committed to producing them.
"We continue to develop our future EVs and work to reduce battery costs," Reuss said during the event. "And when the U.S. market is ready for EVs in large numbers, we will be there for them."
AI development
GM expects to achieve such targets through the use of AI in research and development.
The company said it is developing a "new operating approach for vehicle development" that leans into enterprise AI and virtualization to increase speed.
"This concurrent engineering model allows us to innovate faster, improve continuously, and scale new technologies across our lineup with incredible agility," the company said in a release.
GM used the development of its next-generation vehicles, including a new battery chemistry, as an example of how the new technologies are reshaping its vehicle development.
The company said it virtually tested more than 300,000 battery designs using its recently announced lithium manganese rich battery chemistry, or LMR, before building a single physical prototype.
Anderson said Wednesday that LMR will be the exclusive battery tech for its fourth-generation EVs. GM had previously said it wanted to use those batteries in full-size electric vehicles such as its Chevrolet Silverado and Escalade IQ beginning in 2028.
Anderson said GM is uniquely positioned to use AI compared to other automotive companies because of its more than 100 years in the industry as well as 30 years of OnStar.
"In the age of AI, data is currency," Anderson said. "For decades, GM's engineering, manufacturing and product teams have generated unparalleled body of data that we're now using to build industry-leading AI tools."
In-vehicle AI
The company is building on its internal use of AI to better shape its experiences for customers.
GM on Wednesday reconfirmed that it plans to launch a proprietary in-vehicle AI assistant through its OnStar technology brand.
The OnStar AI assistant is expected to launch in the coming months on the 2027 Cadillac Lyriq EV through an over-the-air update before expanding to other models.
GM currently uses Google's Gemini for its in-vehicle AI assistant. The company told CNBC earlier this year that the GM-developed AI will be more integrated with the vehicle.
The goal for OnStar AI, which will be available through a subscription, is to help customers be productive while in the car, especially if the vehicle has self-driving capabilities that don't require the driver or passengers to monitor the system.
GM on Wednesday also reiterated its plans to launch eyes-off highway driving in 2028. The automaker said a year ago that it wanted to launch that technology. It's been five years since Barra said she expected the automaker to offer personal autonomous vehicles this decade.
"Our vision is that eventually every vehicle should drive itself or its occupants anywhere, and we're investing across the self-driving stack to make that real," Anderson said.

articles.title: Trump-aligned super PACs pour millions into once-safe GOP House seats
articles.text:
President Donald Trump has made good on his claim of having put more than $300 million of his political war chest into the 2026 midterm election.
New campaign finance filings released Tuesday night show millions flowing into House districts that were barely competitive two years ago, underscoring how far the GOP's problems have spread in the final weeks of the campaign.
MAGA Inc., Trump's main super political action committee, reported $300.5 million in disbursements through Oct. 14, with a quarter of that election cycle total — $75.5 million — being spent in the first two weeks of October, according to new Federal Election Commission filings. It still held $164.3 million in cash, and Trump said Tuesday his political operation would spend more than $400 million by Election Day.
Much of the money is moving through two new Trump-aligned groups. MAGA Inc. has sent $200 million to No Going Back PAC and $25 million to Safety & Affordability PAC, which have already reported more than $209 million in independent expenditures between them, according to FEC filings.
The spending is also likely to ease months of Republican anxiety that Trump would sit on his massive war chest rather than deploy it in the midterms. GOP operatives had worried as recently as September that MAGA Inc.'s cash would remain largely on the sidelines.
Safety & Affordability has spent $3.76 million in Arizona's 1st District, $1.84 million in Maine's 2nd, $1.6 million in Wisconsin's 3rd, $1.48 million in North Carolina's 1st and $1.4 million in Ohio's 10th. It has also put more than $1 million each into Pennsylvania's 8th, Ohio's 9th and Michigan's 7th, according to a CNBC analysis of the PAC's filing.
Several are established battlegrounds. The Cook Political Report with Amy Walter rates Wisconsin's 3rd, North Carolina's 1st, Pennsylvania's 8th, Ohio's 9th and Michigan's 7th among its 21 "Toss Up" races.
Other places Trump is donating show Republicans being forced onto less familiar terrain.
In Ohio's 10th District, Safety & Affordability PAC has spent about $1.4 million defending Republican Rep. Mike Turner, who won by 18 points in 2024. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee now lists the seat among a new tier of possible 2026 pickups, while the National Republican Congressional Committee only began spending there this month, according to AdImpact.
No Going Back has also spent roughly $5 million each in Republican-held Michigan's 4th and North Carolina's 11th, while putting another $14.4 million combined into Democratic-held Florida's 14th and 25th, according to a CNBC analysis of the PAC's FEC filing.
At the same time, other Republican groups are beginning to triage. The Congressional Leadership Fund, a super PAC aligned with House Speaker Mike Johnson, stopped spending on advertising in Iowa's 1st, New Jersey's 7th, Michigan's 8th and Ohio's 1st, the Associated Press reported last week. Trump-aligned groups, meanwhile, have spent about $1.4 million across those four races, according to a CNBC analysis of FEC filings.
Republicans still hold the advertising edge in 25 of the 42 House races rated "Toss Up" or "Lean" Republican or Democrat by the Cook Report, according to AdImpact. But the political environment continues to move toward Democrats. Of the 21 House races Cook rates as "Toss Ups," 16 are Republican-held and five are held by Democrats.
Trump's PACs have also spent big in the Senate, according to the new filings. No Going Back has spent nearly $30 million in Michigan, $27.8 million in Ohio, $11.8 million in New Hampshire and $9.9 million in North Carolina, according to a CNBC analysis of the new FEC filings. Those four races alone account for roughly $79 million.
Trump's own standing may help explain the pressure. A New York Times/Siena College poll released Wednesday put his approval rating at 36%, with 59% disapproving.
Voters in the poll disapproved of his handling of the cost of living by 69% to 29% and gas prices by 73% to 24%. Democrats led by 10 points when voters were presented with the House candidates actually running in their districts.
Trump's allies are also trying to solve a turnout problem: getting voters who backed him in presidential elections to show up when he is not on the ballot.
MAGA Inc., in its latest filing, reported a $16.2 million Oct. 8 disbursement labeled "voting education." The New York Times reported Tuesday that the group has run more than 2,200 unique Facebook and Instagram ads in more than 20 states urging Republicans to vote early or turn out.

articles.title: Parents who have the strongest relationships with their kids ask these 5 'revealing' questions, says conversation expert
articles.text:
We've all had moments like these, as both parents and kids: "What did you get up to today?" "Nothing." "How was school today?" "Fine."
Of course, you care about your kid and want to know what's really going on with them. But the problem with questions like these is that they can create an unintentional conversational burden for your child.
After a long day, the last thing they want is another thing to think through. They also might worry that if they answer with anything other than "I'm fine," they'll get a wave of concern from us. That's why many kids dislike these questions or default to "fine" — even if they aren't.
As a behavioral researcher with over a decade of experience studying human conversation and connectedness, I've found that the questions that can give you the clearest sense of your child's emotional state sound like they're about something else on the surface. But the answers tell you a lot about what's going on underneath.
They also have no one "good" or "right" answer that your kid feels like they have to defend. In practice, they should feel like a low-stakes game. You can use these lighter-hearted queries as a ladder to get to heavier topics. Of course, make sure you talk to your child's physician if you have any major concerns about their well-being.
Start with these five questions to help you get the answers you're searching for — and build stronger ties with your kid.
1. 'What's something you're weirdly good at that never comes up?'
This is a great prompt for kids who typically refuse to answer questions. Most of the feedback kids get comes from adults. This question is special because it gives children the chance to compliment themselves, and establish a sense of agency, positivity and pride.
If they name a concrete skill, encourage it. You can also ask a follow-up question like, "How did you figure that out?" or "Can you teach me?" But if they say something along the lines of "Nothing, I guess," they might not give themselves enough credit or feel safe bragging to you. If they draw a blank, name one skill you've noticed in them.
2. 'Which TV, movie or book character is most like you, and why?'
A kid will tell you about themselves through a character. Be sure to ask why they chose that character. Their explanation is more important than your interpretation.
The words they use matter. If they say "funny," "brave" or "loyal," that tells you what they're proud of. Phrases like "nobody sees him" or "she's always left out" might reveal how they feel they're being treated right now.
If they tell you a specific hero or lead, they likely see themselves as the driver of their own story. If they're a sidekick, they might feel a need to downplay their own importance. If they say a villain, don't be alarmed. Plenty of villains are characters who are often misunderstood and your kid might be telling you they feel the same way.
3. 'If your life, or day, had a title like a movie, what would it be?'
This question replaces the more easily dodged "Are you okay?" Kids also tend to love this question because it's more of a game than an obvious probe into their mood — even though it is something of a disguised emotional check-in.
If they offer you a funny title, they are likely in a light-hearted mood. If they give you a bleak or flat title, make a note and then ask a follow-up later that day like, "Why was your movie title 'The Longest Tuesday Ever?'"
With that information, you can open up the lines of communication to help them problem-solve and feel better.
4. 'If you had a totally free day with nothing to do, what would you do without spending any money?'
If they answer "nothing" or "sleeping," they might be uninspired or running on empty. Feel free to skip the pep talk and ask what's been taking up their energy lately. Sometimes "sleeping" just means it's been a really long week.
If they respond with something creative like painting, or social like hanging out with friends, that's a good indication of what boosts their energy, rather than drains it.
When you know what fuels them, look for ways to consistently include it in their routine, like 20 minutes of play after homework or a Saturday craft night with a friend. Let them pick when it happens so they want to continue doing it.
5. 'Who do you feel the most relaxed around? Who makes you feel the most stressed?'
There are many social interactions kids have that parents aren't privy to, especially for school-age children. These questions are revealing because they show when kids' guards go up and down, even when they don't realize it. Your child might be surprised by their own response.
Try your best to not react to their answer. If you flinch at the person who stresses them out, your kid learns what it costs to tell you things. Give them the space to talk about why they feel this way.
Identifying the people and environments that drain them is a valuable skill for kids. They can't always choose who is in their class or family, but they can choose where they devote their energy and who they want to spend their free time with. You can help model that as well.
Ask these questions in the car, at dinner or at bedtime. But make sure not to ask too many in a row, or it'll turn into an interrogation. Take a turn answering them yourself. It demonstrates that you're willing to be open about your feelings, too.
When you stay curious and ask the right questions, eventually your child might bring up the thing that happened before you even have to ask.
Vanessa Van Edwards is a speaker, researcher and the author of "Conversation: How to Connect with Anyone & Make Every Interaction Count," "Captivate: The Science of Succeeding with People″ and "Cues: Master the Secret Language of Charismatic Communication." She is the founder of Science of People, where she leads workshops and courses on science-based soft skills to help people become better communicators.

articles.title: Meta ordered to pay $25 billion penalty in New Mexico Cambridge Analytica case
articles.text:
Meta was ordered to pay $25 billion in penalties by a New Mexico court on Wednesday as part of a data privacy case that stemmed from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal from nearly a decade ago.
The penalty, revealed in a court filing, comes after a jury in a Santa Fe courthouse found in September the social media giant liable for misleading state citizens about how it safeguards and collects user data and prevents harmful information from flourishing on its services.
Although the jury concluded that Meta had more than 43 million violations of the state's unfair practices act, with each transgression carrying a civil penalty as high as $5,000, a New Mexico judge was responsible for determining the ultimate fine. The Wednesday filing showed that the state was awarded $219.5 billion, but the penalty was ultimately reduced to $25 billion.
"The extraordinary number of willful violations found by the jury, the duration and repetition of the conduct, the breadth of subjects on which violations occurred, the involvement of senior Facebook leadership, the size of New Mexico audiences reached, and the clear intentional and systematic nature of Facebook's repeated misstatements established in the trial record support the highest level of penalty allowed by the New Mexico Unfair Practices Act - $5,000 per violation found by the jury," New Mexico District Court Judge Francis Mathew wrote in the filing.
The judge added that interest on the penalty shall accrue at the rate of 15% each year until the fine is paid off in full.
"For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law," said New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez in a statement.
He added that "this penalty order demonstrates that those violations carry real consequences."
Meta chief legal officer C.J. Mahoney criticized the penalty, saying in a statement that the company is "confident" that it will "prevail on appeal."
"This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico," Mahoney said in the statement. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online."
Meta previously resolved various Cambridge Analytica-derived data privacy lawsuits across the nation as part of an overarching August settlement of nearly $17 billion with a coalition of state attorneys general in a separate federal case related to child safety and mental health. But because New Mexico was not part of the settlement, the state's data privacy case that arose from Meta's Cambridge Analytica scandal proceeded to trial in September.
In 2022, the social media giant agreed to pay $725 million to settle a class action lawsuit that also sprang from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal that kicked off in 2018. That scandal rocked the Mark Zuckerberg-led company before its official name change to Meta, and focused on allegations that the political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica improperly accessed the information of 87 million users, raising questions about Facebook's data handling practices.
Mathew said in the filing that "Facebook did not conduct the comprehensive investigation that it promised" following the Cambridge Analytica revelations.
"Pressure from senior executives to keep costs down, lack of adequate enforcement resources, inadequate investigative techniques, and a desire not to create precedent for future investigations," all contributed to what the judge characterized as a "willfully ineffective" internal examination by Facebook, the filing said.
Former New Mexico Attorney General Hector Balderas originally filed the state's Cambridge Analytica-related lawsuit in 2021, while current AG Torrez oversaw the related trial.
Torrez also led his state's child safety-related trial against Meta that resulted in a March jury ruling that the social media company should pay $375 million for violating the state's unfair practices act. A New Mexico judge would later order Meta to pay $567 million into an abatement fund as part of a second phase of the case that determined the social media firm's actions created a public nuisance.
Meta said it disagreed with that New Mexico ruling and planned to appeal.

articles.title: Expanding AI trade is turning safety stocks into a 'Texas hedge'
articles.text:
When a hurricane looms, panic buying clears store shelves of household essentials like water, canned food, dry goods, and toilet paper. A similar dynamic is playing out in the market. Investors are bailing on higher-volatility growth stocks and running toward the shelter of perceived safety sectors like utilities and consumer staples. The key difference? They may not be so safe.
As valuation multiples across capital-intensive AI infrastructure plays — such as specialized data center hosting providers CoreWeave (CRWV) and Iren Ltd (IREN) — take on water in the form of massive debt loads due to aggressive capex buildouts, investors may want to take a portion of their equity exposure into more protected water. The issue with utilities is that while it is traditionally considered a conservative sector, more recently it has become part of the AI story as the massive data center build-out is accompanied by surging power demand. This is one of the reasons that in recent years utilities outperformed staples. However, if the bloom of the AI rose helped fuel that outperformance, it would be a “Texas hedge” to buy it now on concerns that the AI trade is getting wobbly. In other words, buying so-called safety stocks might actually increase your risk.
In this context, consumer staples, most easily traded with the Consumer Staples Select Sector SPDR Fund (XLP) is a better choice.
Unlike AI infrastructure, hyperscalers are dependent on enterprise IT budgets and continuous capital infusions. XLP's constituents—led by market heavyweights like Walmart (WMT), the world’s largest grocery store chain, Costco (COST), a perennial “Holly Index” constituent, Procter & Gamble (PG), and toilet paper and diaper maker Kimberly-Clark — generate consistent revenues. I often joke that when the market goes sideways, investors probably need more diapers and toilet paper, not less. Plainly put, consumers buy toothpaste, groceries, and cleaning supplies regardless of macro or micro economic stress.
Consumer staples tend to deliver steady cash flow and XLP distributes a lot of that back to shareholders with a ~2.6% annualized dividend yield. This provides an organic return buffer during market pullbacks, contrasting sharply with high-beta data center operators that re-invest every dollar into equipment and facilities.
Leveraged AI hosts trade at elevated multiples, leaving minimal room for execution errors. Consumer staples offer lower beta (read lower downside in a general equity market pullback).
Options strategy: bullish call diagonal spread
To capture a structural rotation into staples over a horizon extending into early 2027, a long call diagonal is capital efficient and risk-defined.
- Buy January 2027 $85.00 Call: (these are in-the-money) With a ~0.65–0.70 delta, these calls provides a more stock-like exposure for considerably less than purchasing the stock outright (one does sacrifice dividends versus the stock), but this also reduces the “extrinsic” premium associated with buying them - thus less decay or “theta”.
- Sell November $92.00 Call: Assuming these expire worthless one could further monetize short-term upside movements by repeatedly selling out-of-the-money upside calls against the longer-dated position to lower the net cost basis over time. Assuming the long calls remain in the money by expiration the calls can be exercised and one would own the underlying shares.
Risk & reward summary
- Max Risk: Capped strictly at the initial net debit paid for the options strategy.
- Max Gain: Achieved if XLP trends steadily toward the 92–95 target by the nearer dated expiration, are unlimited if the nearer dated options expire worthless and no new short upside call options are sold against the longer-dated calls.
- Strategic Fit: Reallocates capital away from over-leveraged tech exposure into defensive, cash-flow positive staples.

articles.title: Hoa hậu Quỳnh Anh không được thi Miss Universe
articles.text:
Hoa hậu Quỳnh Anh không được thi Miss Universe
Sau loạt ồn ào hậu đăng quang Miss Universe Vietnam 2026, Quỳnh Anh tiếp tục nhận thêm tin không vui.
- 14-10-2026Bạn trai Hoa hậu Quỳnh Anh làm gì thế này?
- 14-10-2026Hoa hậu Quỳnh Anh lên tiếng giữa ồn ào lộ nhóm chat nói xấu Kỳ Duyên
- 13-10-2026Vừa đăng quang 10 ngày, Hoa hậu Quỳnh Anh đã phải xin lỗi
Sau loạt ồn ào hậu đăng quang, Hoa hậu Quỳnh Anh tiếp tục đối mặt với tin không vui khi sẽ không thể góp mặt tại Miss Universe 2026. Không chỉ Việt Nam, đại diện của 5 quốc gia Đông Nam Á khác cũng rơi vào tình cảnh tương tự.
Theo thông tin được công bố bởi tổ chức của ông Nawat, các đại diện Việt Nam, Thái Lan, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore và Lào chưa được tổ chức Miss Universe công nhận đủ điều kiện tham gia mùa giải lần thứ 75, dự kiến diễn ra tại Puerto Rico vào tháng 11/2026.
Trong thông báo, ông Nawat nhấn mạnh, MGI không chấp nhận việc quyền bản quyền bị đơn phương vô hiệu hóa, phản đối việc thí sinh trở thành bên chịu thiệt. Phía ông Nawat tuyên bố việc 6 đại diện không đến cuộc thi không đồng nghĩa với việc công ty tự nguyện rút lui, từ bỏ quyền hợp đồng hay chấp nhận quyết định chấm dứt những quyền đó.
Suốt thời gian qua, mâu thuẫn giữa ông Nawat Itsaragrisil - người quản lý bản quyền Miss Universe khu vực phía đông - và ông Raul Rocha - người nắm giữ 50% cổ phần MUO - liên tục được đẩy lên cao trào, từ quyền cấp phép cuộc thi tại các quốc gia đến thẩm quyền điều hành, phát ngôn và quản lý thương hiệu.
Theo các thông cáo được công bố trước đó, phía JKN Universe LLC từng cho rằng các thỏa thuận nhượng quyền tại Việt Nam và một số nước Đông Nam Á do đơn vị liên quan đến ông Nawat ký kết không có cơ sở cấp phép hợp lệ. Phía này khẳng định MU East không có thẩm quyền cấp hoặc chuyển giao quyền nhượng quyền thương hiệu tại những thị trường nói trên.
Ngược lại, MU East lập tức phản bác, cho rằng JKN Universe LLC thuộc sở hữu chung theo tỷ lệ 50:50 giữa MU East và MU West thông qua JKN Legacy Inc. MU East khẳng định mình có quyền vận hành, phát triển thương hiệu và quản lý các đối tác nhượng quyền tại 95 lãnh thổ thuộc khu vực phía Đông.
Hai phía liên tục đưa ra thông cáo để bảo vệ lập trường của mình, khiến công chúng phải tự đối chiếu từng tuyên bố. Trước đó, ông Nawat thông báo Việt Nam sẽ là quốc gia đăng cai Miss Universe 2027 trên Fanpage. Nhưng không lâu sau đó, tổ chức Miss Universe dùng kênh Instagram để phủ nhận thông tin trên. Những bất đồng trong việc quản lý cuộc thi khiến fan sắc đẹp thở dài, đồng thời khiến uy tín cuộc thi ngày càng đi xuống.
Hiện tại, vẫn chưa rõ Quỳnh Anh có cơ hội tham dự Miss Universe vào năm 2027 hay không. Khi tranh chấp bản quyền giữa các bên chưa được giải quyết, tương lai của đại diện Việt Nam vẫn là dấu hỏi lớn.
Tại chung kết Miss Universe Vietnam 2026 diễn ra đầu tháng 10, Quỳnh Anh vượt qua các thí sinh còn lại để giành vương miện, song kết quả và phần trả lời ứng xử của tân Hoa hậu cũng vấp phải những ý kiến trái chiều.
Chưa dừng lại ở đó, sau đăng quang, những đoạn tin nhắn được cho là trích từ một nhóm chat riêng, có nội dung nhắc đến một số nhân vật trong giới sắc đẹp, tiếp tục khiến cô trở thành tâm điểm tranh luận.
Trước phản ứng của dư luận, Quỳnh Anh đã lên tiếng xin lỗi, đồng thời được cho là chủ động nhắn tin xin lỗi riêng những người liên quan.

articles.title: New Mexico AG lawsuit accuses Epstein's attorney and accountant of facilitating sex trafficking
articles.text:
New Mexico's attorney general on Wednesday filed a federal lawsuit accusing Jeffrey Epstein's long-time personal lawyer and accountant of facilitating Epstein's sex trafficking operation.
The civil suit alleges the attorney, Darren Indyke, and the accountant, Richard Kahn, helped finance and conceal Epstein's sex trafficking, which included the abuse of girls and young women at his Zorro Ranch in Santa Fe County, New Mexico.
Indyke and Kahn are beneficiaries of Epstein's 1953 Trust, co-executors of Epstein's estate, and administrators of the revocable trust, whose name comes from the year of the convicted sex offender's birth.
New Mexico's suit asks a judge to block Indyke and Kahn from receiving payments from the estate as the case proceeds in U.S. District Court in New Mexico.
The suit alleges the two men participated in a sex trafficking venture in violation of the federal Trafficking Victims Protection Act; and that they violated New Mexico's Racketeering Act by engaging in kidnapping, criminal solicitation and conspiracy.
Attorney General Raul Torrez's office said Epstein's estate is currently valued at more than $107 million, and the suit says Indyke and Kahn are eligible for bequests of $50 million and $25 million, subject to the availability of funds.
"Jeffrey Epstein did not operate alone, and his death does not end the pursuit of accountability for the people who helped make his crimes possible," Torrez said in a statement, which was released as he appeared at a press conference flanked by two survivors of abuse by Epstein, Anouska De Georgiou and Julia Molchanova.
"The allegations in this lawsuit describe a network of people and financial arrangements that helped sustain and conceal the abuse of vulnerable girls and young women, including here in New Mexico," Torrez said. "Those who allegedly enabled this exploitation should not be allowed to profit from it while survivors continue to live with its consequences."
The suit comes a month after The Wall Street Journal reported that the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York had opened an investigation into Indyke and Kahn.
De Georgiou said at the press conference that her abuse by Epstein and his accomplice, Ghislaine Maxwell, "did not happen in isolation."
"It could not have continued for as long as it did without people facilitating it, looking the other way, or choosing to do nothing to stop it," De Georgiou said. "Accountability cannot end with Epstein and Maxwell. It must extend to those who knowingly made their abuse possible, especially those who stand to profit from it. That includes anyone who knowingly helped make Epstein appear legitimate to conceal his abuse of women and girls."
Daniel Weiner, an attorney for Epstein's estate, in a statement to CNBC, said, "Both Mr. Indyke and Mr. Kahn reject as categorically false the allegations that they knowingly facilitated or assisted Mr. Epstein in his sexual abuse or trafficking of women, or that they were aware of Mr. Epstein's actions while they provided legal or accounting services to him."
"They are confident that they will prevail on the claims asserted against them," Weiner said.
"Neither the New Mexico Attorney General nor anyone from his office asked to speak with Mr. Indyke or Mr. Kahn to seek relevant information from them before filing this baseless lawsuit, raising serious questions about the thoroughness of the Attorney General's investigation and the motivations for his lawsuit," Weiner said.
"Messrs. Indyke and Kahn have given multiple depositions in civil lawsuits and have testified at length before the U.S. House of Representatives Committee on Oversight and Government Reform," the attorney said. "Had the New Mexico Attorney General wanted to learn the actual facts of their professional services for Epstein, the Attorney General or his staff could have reached out to schedule interviews. Messrs. Indyke and Kahn have cooperated with any and all investigations when asked to do so."
The lawsuit alleges Indyke and Kahn personally profited from their relationship to Epstein, who killed himself in a federal jail in New York in August 2019, weeks after being arrested on child sex trafficking charges.
"Between 2011 and 2019, Indyke received more than $16 million from Epstein and related entities, and Kahn received more than $10 million," Torrez's office said in a statement.
Torrez, at a press conference Wednesday, said his office is continuing a criminal investigation of Epstein's sex trafficking operation. No criminal charges have been filed in connection with that probe.
Epstein's estate in February agreed to pay out as much as $35 million to settle a class action lawsuit in U.S. District Court in Manhattan that accused Indyke and Kahn of aiding and abetting Epstein's sex trafficking.
The proposed settlement does not include any admission of misconduct by Indyke or Kahn. The judge handling the case last month endorsed a proposal by the suit's plaintiff to notify potential class members to submit claims on the settlement by conducting a four-week-long social media campaign on Facebook and Instagram.

articles.title: Triệt phá đường dây tiêu thụ 400 tấn lợn bệnh, lợn chết, thu lợi hơn 10 tỷ đồng
articles.text:
Triệt phá đường dây tiêu thụ 400 tấn lợn bệnh, lợn chết, thu lợi hơn 10 tỷ đồng
Số lợn bệnh, lợn chết được nhóm đối tượng do Trần Văn Hùng cầm đầu thu mua từ nhiều nguồn khác nhau, sau đó vận chuyển, giết mổ và bán làm thực phẩm.
- 21-10-2026Bên trong loạt tủ đông của đường dây do Trần Văn Hùng SN 1975 cầm đầu
- 21-10-2026Triệt phá đường dây tiêu thụ 400 tấn heo bệnh, thu lợi bất chính hơn 10 tỷ đồng
Ngày 21/10, Công an TP Đồng Nai thông tin, Phòng Cảnh sát điều tra tội phạm về tham nhũng, kinh tế, buôn lậu, môi trường (Phòng Cảnh sát Kinh tế, Công an thành phố) đã triệt phá đường dây thu gom, giết mổ lợn bệnh, lợn chết với quy mô lớn để đưa ra thị trường tiêu thụ.
Đường dây do Trần Văn Hùng (sinh năm 1975, ngụ khu phố Xuân Hiệp, phường Xuân Lộc, thành phố Đồng Nai) cầm đầu.
Theo điều tra, đầu tháng 9/2026, qua các biện pháp nghiệp vụ, Phòng Cảnh sát Kinh tế phát hiện đường dây chuyên thu gom, vận chuyển, giết mổ lợn bệnh, lợn chết để bán làm thực phẩm cho người tại phường Xuân Lộc, xã Xuân Hòa và các khu vực lân cận. Nhóm đối tượng thu mua lợn từ nhiều nguồn, sau đó vận chuyển, giết mổ và đưa ra thị trường tiêu thụ. Cơ quan công an đã xác lập chuyên án để đấu tranh.
Ngày 5/10/2026, dưới sự chỉ đạo của Thiếu tướng Nguyễn Đức Hải, Giám đốc Công an thành phố Đồng Nai, Ban chuyên án huy động lực lượng đồng loạt kiểm tra 5 địa điểm liên quan, gồm: điểm trung chuyển lợn, cơ sở kinh doanh và địa điểm giết mổ của Trần Văn Hùng, cơ sở sản xuất giò chả của Phạm Thị Hân trên địa bàn phường Xuân Lộc; địa điểm bán thịt lợn của Nguyễn Thị Thu Phượng trước cổng khu công nghiệp Xuân Lộc.
Tại các địa điểm kiểm tra, lực lượng công an thu giữ khoảng 7 tấn thịt lợn nhiễm virus dịch tả lợn châu Phi cùng nhiều tang vật liên quan.
Kết quả điều tra ban đầu xác định, từ năm 2024, Hùng cùng vợ là Huỳnh Thị Hiếu Em tổ chức thu mua lợn bệnh, lợn chết từ các cá nhân, điểm thu gom và trạm trung chuyển. Số lợn này được đưa về khu vực giết mổ tại phường Xuân Lộc để pha lóc thành thịt nạc, thịt ba chỉ, thịt đùi; phần da, mỡ tiếp tục được chế biến để bán.
Quá trình hoạt động, Hùng thuê Trịnh Thanh Lâm (sinh năm 1987, quê tỉnh An Giang) làm tài xế điều khiển xe ô tô biển kiểm soát 60M-5313 (xe của Hùng) đi thu mua lợn chết và vận chuyển về địa điểm giết mổ của Hùng. Tại đây, Hùng và Hiếu Em chỉ đạo các nhân công là Lê Quốc Phó (sinh năm 2000, quê tỉnh An Giang), Nguyễn Thành Trung (sinh năm 2005, quê tỉnh Lâm Đồng) và Nguyễn Hồng Phúc (sinh năm 2002, quê tỉnh Đồng Nai) cả 3 đều tạm trú phường Xuân Lộc, thực hiện mổ, pha lóc thành các phần thịt ba chỉ, thịt nạc, thịt đùi để Hiếu Em giao cho con gái là Trần Thị Cẩm Bào (sinh năm 1992, ngụ phường Xuân Lộc) liên hệ, bán cho Nguyễn Thị Thu Phượng (sinh năm 1975, ngụ xã Xuân Hòa) với giá từ 25.000 đồng đến 40.000 đồng/kg.
Thịt lợn chết sau khi mua, Phượng bán trực tiếp cho người dân tại khu vực cổng Khu công nghiệp Xuân Lộc và cung cấp cho Phạm Thị Hân với giá từ 35.000 đến 55.000 đồng/kg để sản xuất giò chả. Cơ quan điều tra xác định các đối tượng biết rõ nguồn gốc lợn bệnh, lợn chết, nhưng vẫn đưa đi chế biến, tiêu thụ.
Cơ quan công an xác định, từ năm 2024 đến nay, các đối tượng đã thu mua, giết mổ khoảng 400 tấn lợn bệnh, lợn chết để tiêu thụ làm thực phẩm, thu lợi bất chính hơn 10 tỷ đồng.
Cơ quan Cảnh sát điều tra Công an TP Đồng Nai đã khởi tố vụ án, khởi tố bị can, bắt tạm giam 9 đối tượng gồm: Trần Văn Hùng, Trịnh Thanh Lâm, Huỳnh Thị Hiếu Em, Trần Thị Cẩm Bào, Nguyễn Thị Thu Phượng, Lê Quốc Phó, Nguyễn Hồng Phúc, Nguyễn Thành Trung và Phạm Thị Hân về tội “Vi phạm quy định về an toàn thực phẩm” tại Điều 317 Bộ luật Hình sự.
Qua vụ việc, Công an TP Đồng Nai khuyến cáo các tổ chức, cá nhân hoạt động sản xuất, chế biến, kinh doanh thực phẩm nghiêm túc chấp hành các quy định của pháp luật về an toàn thực phẩm; không vì lợi nhuận mà thực hiện hành vi gian dối, xâm phạm quyền lợi người tiêu dùng.
Người dân cần lựa chọn thực phẩm có nguồn gốc, xuất xứ rõ ràng, chủ động cung cấp thông tin cho cơ quan Công an khi phát hiện dấu hiệu vi phạm, góp phần cùng lực lượng chức năng bảo đảm an toàn thực phẩm và sức khỏe cộng đồng.
